en: Commentary on the *Sūtra on Examining the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma*, Scroll One.
Translated by the Foreign Śramaṇa Bodhidharmottara of the Sui Dynasty;
composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu.
The scripture consists of three parts. From "Thus have I heard" up to "Therefore, I now cause him to speak it" constitutes the introductory section.

From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith, having understood the Buddha’s intention" up to the end of the lower fascicle and the offerings made to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha constitutes the main exposition section. From "At that time, the Buddha addressed the great [Bodhisattvas]"... [text continues].
The assembly, having attained profound faith, received [the teaching], and practiced it accordingly. This is the section on circulation (*pravartana*).

The introductory section consists of two parts: first, the section on attestation of faith (*samyaksambodhi-śraddhā-pratītya*), and second, the section on the occasion of the teaching’s inception (*nidāna*).
Now, for the first: Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat, the Omniscient One, was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
In the midst of the mountains, by means of his supernormal powers, he manifested a vast, magnificent, pure, and unobstructed site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Together with an immeasurable and boundless great assembly, he expounded the profound Dharma-gate of the Collection of Roots.
"Thus" refers to the essence of the Dharma as it has been heard; that is, its being exactly as it is within the single, true realm, without error.
"I" refers to Ānanda’s partial realization of the virtues of the Dharmakāya—wisdom, liberation, permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and his attainment of the eight masteries.
He is neither a self nor a non-self; he is designated by the conventional name "I" in accordance with worldly usage. [He] heard.
Ānanda thoroughly realized that the nature of the faculties, the nature of sound, and the nature of consciousness are all a single reality-realm (*ekasatya-viṣaya*).
Subject and object are perfectly interfused; it is neither hearing nor non-hearing, yet it is called "hearing.

As for "at one time," it refers to the perfect resonance and perfect response, wherein beginning and end do not transcend the present single thought-moment. "Bhagavān, the Omniscient One" refers to ultimate perfection.

The World-Honored One of Great Enlightenment, who has realized the realm of the single reality, is the Teacher manifested within the hearts of all sentient beings, brought forth by their shared roots of goodness. In Sanskrit, he is called *Bhagavān*, also translated as *Bhagavat*.
Because it possesses six meanings, it is not translated [into Chinese]; rather, it is a title that encompasses all supreme virtues. Thus, he is the Tathāgata.
Because he is never bound by any afflictions, he possesses the sense of mastery (*vaśitā*). Because he is refined and tempered by the blazing fire of wisdom, he possesses the sense of intensity.
Because he is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, he possesses the sense of sublime beauty.
Because all supreme qualities are perfected and there is nothing he has not heard, he possesses [the sense of...]
It possesses the meaning of renown, for it is praised by all the world who draw near to it and make offerings.

It possesses the meaning of auspiciousness, for its own benefit is fulfilled and it constantly applies skillful means to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings without ever ceasing.
It possesses the meaning of nobility, for it perfects the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and, within the single reality of the object—
Whether the realms be provisional or ultimate, he has investigated them to their very depths with complete clarity; there is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see.
For this reason, he is called the "All-Knowing One" (Sarvajña). As for Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha: "Rājagṛha" is called Rājagṛha in Sanskrit;
it is within the territory of Central India and was the capital of King Ajātaśatru. "Gṛdhrakūṭa" translates here as "Spiritual" (or "Holy").

The Vulture Peak: Three or four *li* to the northeast of the city of Rājagṛha, this city and this mountain are the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) transformed by the seeds of the mutual cognition of all sentient beings dwelling therein;
that is to say, they are the objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*) of each individual’s own eighth consciousness.
They serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*) for one another, acting as mutual substantial bases (*bimba*) and reflected images (*pratibimba*), in harmonious combination.
They appear as one, yet in reality each obtains the whole to serve as their environment and retribution; they are neither mixed nor obstructed.

As for the All-Knowing One being also within it: by the power of great compassion, in response to those capable of being transformed, he does not depart from the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, yet manifests the appearance of the defiled land where ordinary beings and sages dwell. If this very defiled land were...

Within the realm of sentient beings, these are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) objective portions; if they were within the realm of the Buddhas, they would be the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objective portions.

As for manifesting this vast, pure, and unobstructed site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) through the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), this very Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) is originally manifested by the mind alone.
It takes the mind as its substance; outside the mind there is no mountain, for the mind is vast.
Because the mind is vast, the mountain is also vast; because the mind is pure and adorned, the mountain is also pure and adorned; because the mind is unobstructed, the mountain is also unobstructed.
This vastness is the measure of its nature, equal in extent to empty space, for it is free from all marks; this is the virtue of *prajñā*.
This purity and adornment is the inherent endowment of its nature, possessing boundless virtues and being identical with all phenomena; this is *vimukti*.
Virtue. Non-obstruction is the essence of its nature. This essence unifies both concealment and illumination; it is neither empty nor existent, for it is not obstructed by emptiness or existence.
Thus, it is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body is permanence, liberation is stillness, and prajñā is radiance.

It is, in truth, the Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance, the wondrous realm of inherent virtue. Sentient beings are deluded by it, perceiving it instead as the defiled land of cohabitation (*sahā-loka*). Regarding this—

The Buddha’s constant dwelling is the vast, pure, and unobstructed site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Having fulfilled the cultivation of virtue, he eternally enjoys the Dharma-bliss that accords with his nature;

it is also called the "Superior Pure Land of True Retribution. Beyond both demonstration and non-demonstration, the Buddha now employs the power of his spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) to empower a certain class of sentient beings so that they may turn back from delusion and return to awakening, enabling them to behold it.

Thus, this is not departing from the Land of Common Residence (sahā-loka-dhātu), yet one perceives the Land of Enjoyment for Others (saṃbhoga-kāya) horizontally; hence it is called "manifestation" (śi).

"Divine" (shen) refers to the naturally unfathomable essence, which is the virtue of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya-guṇa). "Pervasive" (tong) refers to the unimpeded wisdom of illumination, which is the virtue of Prajñā.
"Power" (li) refers to the capacity for sovereign transformation, which is the virtue of Liberation (vimukti). These arise from within the minds of all Buddhas.
Because sentient beings have cultivated merit and achieved spiritual efficacy, they are able to evoke the Buddha within their own minds, who manifests as a wondrous realm.

Because the Buddha-nature and its virtues within the minds of sentient beings are perfectly realized, the Buddhas within their own minds respond to them, enabling them to see the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This very site of enlightenment, when situated within the sphere of the Buddhas, is...
Regarding the aspect of the object (nimittabhāga) that is untainted (anāsrava): if it were within the category of sentient beings, it would be an aspect of the object that is tainted (sāsrava).
Therefore, while they coexist in the defiled land (saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra), the fundamental substance (mūlaprakṛti) of sentient beings is always tainted;

however, the aspect of the object manifested by the Buddha, based upon the tainted fundamental substance of sentient beings, is always untainted, because it is identical in nature to the transforming consciousness (pariṇāmavijñāna) which is itself untainted. Thus, there is no obstruction.
Regarding the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): the fundamental substance (*svabhāva*) of the Buddhas is eternally untainted (*anāsrava*).

Sentient beings rely upon the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) manifested from the Buddhas' untainted fundamental substance, which is eternally tainted (*sāsrava*), because it shares the same nature as the transforming consciousnesses (*pariṇāmavijñāna*) that are tainted.
Apart from the minds of the Buddhas and sentient beings, neither the tainted nor the untainted—whether as substance or as reflection—can be apprehended. Therefore, it is said:

All is but mind; it is solely the realm of the single reality. Regarding the phrase "together with an immeasurable and boundless great assembly," this refers to the audience who hear the teaching together.
As for this great assembly: if they have already realized the nature of co-arising (*sahaja-gotra*), they share in the same untainted state (*anāsrava*) as the Buddhas;
if they still abide in the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-gotra*), they belong to the same category as all sentient beings.
Regarding those with outflows (*sāsrava*): one should understand that "co-natured" (*sahaja*) refers to those who have attained the full dwelling of a distinct stage or higher.

If they are fully established in the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the three stages of the worthy (*kṣānti*), or above—whether eight people or more—including those in the *piṭaka* of the four fruits and the *pratyekabuddhas*, they are termed "co-natured" in relation to the partial truth (*tattva*).

However, in relation to this single ultimate reality (*eka-tattva*), they are still termed "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). [The Buddha] then expounded the profound Dharma-gate of the aggregate of faculties (*indriya-rāśi*).

This refers to what has already been explained. Although the Sanskrit original is in the future tense, according to the subsequent text, it refers to the *Ṣaḍindriyasaṃgraha-sūtra*, which should be understood as the practice of being complete and without deficiency as clarified in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, and also as the method for purifying the six sense organs as clarified in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*.
This is because, deluded regarding the single reality realm (*ekasatya-viṣaya*), the six sense organs are illusorily formed; accordingly, each one...
The faculties (*indriya*). There is not a single phenomenon that does not tend toward them. The eye is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

it fully gives rise to the ten realms, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses, and the three thousand natures and characteristics, without deficiency or remainder. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so.
Therefore, they are called the "assemblage of faculties. This very assemblage of faculties is entirely formed by encompassing the one true realm. That is to say...
Furthermore, it is called "profound" because it fully embodies the great function of the single reality realm.

This very profound root-mass is able to give rise to sentient beings' understanding and maintains its own nature; therefore, it is called "Dharma. Since this Dharma can lead one through, it is further called a "gate.
Out of concern that those of dull faculties in the final age might be unable to believe and understand when this Dharma is expounded, [it is taught] so as not to cause them to...
Because doubt and regret arise regarding the single reality realm, the Bodhisattva Jiaojingxin (Firm Pure Faith) again offers a solemn request.

One should know that this constitutes the introductory section for the arousal [of the teaching], just as when one wishes to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one first preaches the *Anantārtha-sūtra*.

II. The Introductory Section for the Arousal [of the Teaching] has two parts: A. The Brief Request; B. The Formal Inquiry. In part A, the Brief Request, there are two sections: 1. The Request; 2. [The Response].
The first [chapter] begins here.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dṛḍhaśraddhā (Firm Pure Faith). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to ask a question within this assembly; I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to inquire."
"Venerable One, I pray that you will grant me your hearing and permission.

Because I myself possess firm and pure faith in the realm of the single reality (*eka-tattva*), and am further able to cause others to possess firm and pure faith, I am called the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith (*Dṛḍha-śuddhādhimukti*).
To explain this analytically: the 'correct cause' (*hetu*) is termed 'firm,' while the 'conditional cause' (*pratyaya*) is termed 'pure.'"

The "revealing cause" (*vidyā-hetu*) is called faith. These two causes—the revealing and the conditional—both rely upon the "true cause" (*tathatā-hetu*), and because they cannot be destroyed, it is called "firm and pure faith.

As for "baring the right shoulder": in terms of the phenomenal interpretation (*sāmurti-vyākhyā*), this signifies respectful compliance; in terms of the ultimate interpretation (*paramārtha-vyākhyā*), it signifies the manifestation of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
As for "joining the palms and addressing the Buddha": in terms of the phenomenal interpretation, this signifies single-mindedness; in terms of the ultimate interpretation... [text fragment]

If one understands this, then the provisional and the ultimate are perfectly integrated, converging solely upon the Great Awakening. To seek permission for an inquiry is a constant custom in the Western Regions (India);

whenever one wishes to ask something, one must invariably request leave to do so. This is not like the practices here in this land, where people are reckless and impulsive, entirely lacking in respectful decorum. 2. Granting Permission.
The Buddha said, "Good son, speak as you wish regarding your questions.
An omniscient one answers whatever is asked; from those below the Buddha, none are able to do so.
Therefore, when people questioned Śāriputra, Pūrṇa, and others, they would simply say: 'If I knew this, I would answer according to my ability.'"

[End of section] △ Second, the actual inquiry, which has two parts: first, the inquiry regarding the Dharma; second, the inquiry regarding the person. The first part [the inquiry regarding the Dharma] has two sections:

first, stating the Buddha’s words to pose the question; second, the Buddha pointing to the person as the answer. The first of these [stating the Buddha’s words] also has two parts: first, the direct statement of the Buddha’s words; second, posing the question on behalf of the assembly. This is the first [the direct statement].

The Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith said: "As the Buddha previously taught: when I have passed away, after the True Dharma has been extinguished and the Semblance Dharma is nearing its end, entering the final age—at such a time as this, sentient beings will have meager merit and much suffering and affliction;
the lands will be frequently in turmoil and calamities will arise repeatedly; beset by various misfortunes and terrors, my disciples will lose their..."
They cultivate only wholesome thoughts that increase greed, anger, jealousy, and pride.

Even if they engage in practices resembling the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, they do so solely for the sake of worldly gain and fame, making these their primary concern; they are unable to single-mindedly practice the methods for transcendence.

At that time, sentient beings behold the calamities and chaos of the world, and their minds are constantly timid and weak; they are filled with anxiety and fear for themselves and their kinsmen, unable to find [peace].

Clothing and food merely sustain their physical lives. Due to such numerous obstructive causes and conditions, those with dull faculties and little faith within the Buddha-dharma are extremely few who attain the Way;
even gradually, among those of the three vehicles, those who achieve faith are likewise exceedingly rare.
As for all those who practice and study worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and develop various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they themselves—

Those who possess knowledge of past lives will, in succession, cease to exist. Thus, after a long period has passed within the subsequent Age of Dharma Decline (*mappō*), there will be a total absence of those who attain the Way, acquire faith, or master meditative concentration, supernatural powers, and the various karmic accomplishments.
Meager merit is the cause of decline, affliction, and calamity. Decline, affliction, and calamity are the conditions for losing one's wholesome mindfulness.

Losing mindfulness is the cause for prolonging greed and the pursuit of profit while failing to cultivate the path of transcendence. Failing to cultivate the path of transcendence is the condition for being timid, dull-witted, and lacking in faith.
Therefore, not only can one fail to attain the true path of the One Vehicle, [but one also fails to escape the cycle of suffering].

Furthermore, they are unable to establish the provisional faith of the Three Vehicles. Not only are they unable to cultivate the provisional and ultimate teachings that transcend the world, they are also unable to cultivate worldly meditative concentrations and the karma of supernormal powers.

This is what is meant by the decrease in the number of gods and humans, and the filling of the three evil realms. Question: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and great power. Why is this so?
One cannot save those in this final age of decadence. Answer: It is like the brilliant sun in the midst of the sky; it cannot cause that which is beneath an overturned basin to receive its light.
Though they are equally situated within the vast emptiness of space, they naturally create their own obstructions and separations;
this is not the fault of the brilliant sun. All sentient beings are likewise so: though they are together within the single reality of the ultimate realm, they [create their own barriers].

Because they are shrouded by the illusory obscurations of ignorance, they falsely perceive and are disturbed within the vast, pure, and unobstructed site of enlightenment, giving rise to sorrow and fear.
Thus, regarding the Tathāgata’s realization of the samādhi of the momentary limit (*kṣaṇakoṭi*), they falsely perceive shifting flux as the "end times.
Now, through the power of compassion and vows, I inquire after the skillful means for their sake.

It acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). If one relies upon this Dharma and removes the covering bowl of ignorance, one will behold the Buddha-sun naturally present within the vast space of one's own mind.
△ Second, posing a question on behalf of the assembly.
I now ask the Tathāgata on behalf of those in this future evil age when the Semblance Dharma is nearing its end, and during the Final Dharma, for those who possess even a slight root of goodness.
What skillful means should be employed to instruct, transform, and guide them so that they may give rise to faith and eliminate their decline and afflictions?
For those sentient beings encounter an evil time with many obstacles, which causes them to retreat from their wholesome resolve regarding the world.

Within the mundane and supramundane laws of cause and effect, they frequently give rise to doubts and hesitations, unable to cultivate a firm resolve to seek the wholesome Dharma with single-minded dedication.

Such sentient beings are pitiable and worthy of salvation. O World-Honored One, endowed with great compassion and the knowledge of all modes, we pray that you will employ skillful means to instruct and enlighten them, causing them to leave the net of doubt behind, remove all obstacles, and increase their faith, so that they may follow whichever vehicle is appropriate for them.
They will swiftly attain non-retrogression.

Those with deep roots of goodness will surely achieve liberation early on during the periods of the True Dharma or the Semblance Dharma, so as not to encounter the exhaustion of the Dharma or the times of the final age.
As for those without roots of goodness, even if they should happen to meet the True Dharma or the Semblance Dharma, [they will not be saved].
They have not yet even seen or heard [of this], let alone being in the Dharma-ending age; by what means could they be delivered?

Now, it is precisely because those with a small amount of wholesome roots encounter obstacles that easily cause them to regress, that I specifically seek expedient means to compassionately rescue them. This is due to the abundance of hindrances.

Therefore, they are pitiable; yet because they possess even a slight root of goodness, they can be saved. Great Compassion encompasses pity for all beings—how much more so those who possess even a small root of goodness?
As for the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñatā*), there is no phenomenon it does not know;
how then could it find it difficult to save them from this deceptive web of doubt? However, if one truly lacks roots of goodness, then although Great Compassion pities them, [it cannot save them].
There is no means by which they can be saved. Unless one possesses the wisdom of all modes (*sarvajñā*), even if roots of goodness exist, there is no way to resolve their doubts.

Thus we know that the response of the Buddha and the resonance of the practitioner are mutually related, each possessing its own full power; this does not arise from a single thought, yet it is not produced through co-arising.

As for those who follow any of the vehicles, [the Buddha] establishes the provisional based on the ultimate; one must not cling to the one alone. "Swiftly attaining non-retrogression" refers to the opening of the provisional.
To reveal the reality, there is ultimately no fixed triad. The first section, describing the Buddha’s words and concluding the inquiry, is finished. II. The Buddha points to people as the answer.
The Buddha addressed Dṛḍhaśuddhādhimukti, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have asked well about this matter; it deeply accords with my own intention. Now, regarding this..."
Within this assembly, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Kṣitigarbha. You should inquire about this matter of him;
he shall establish skillful means for you and explain it in detail, fulfilling your aspirations.
"Excellent!"—this praises his swift inquiry into this matter, which accommodates the various capacities of sentient beings below.

"Excellent!"—this praises its profound suitability to my own intent, which accords with the Buddha’s purpose above. Because all phenomena depend upon it for their support and establishment, it is called "Earth" (*bhūmi*).
Because it contains much while remaining without accumulation, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*). This Earth is the "Mind-Earth," which is able to carry [all things].

It is capable of generating. "Treasury" (zàng) refers to the "nature-treasury" (xìng-zàng), which can be brought forth (qùshēng) and can be received within (nà). There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; this is called "bringing forth.

There is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm; this is called "receiving within. Furthermore, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses are termed the "treasury of principle" (lǐ-zàng).
The six perfections, the four immeasurables, the four means of integration, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are termed...

Regarding the practice-treasury (*xingzàng*): within each individual principle-treasury (*lizàng*), there is a practice-treasury. Thus, principle is termed "ground" (*di*) and practice is termed "treasury" (*zàng*).
When each individual practice-treasury simultaneously realizes the principle-treasury, then practice is termed "ground" and principle is termed "treasury.

Furthermore, this is solely the realm of the single reality (*yishi jingjie*); it is termed "ground" in the sense of supporting and carrying, and it is termed "treasury" in the sense of containing and encompassing.
It is a treasury. Within the very essence of the single mind-nature (*cittatā*), there are these two meanings of "sustaining" and "containing.

To realize this essence and its function is what is meant by "Earth Treasury" (*Kṣitigarbha*). Furthermore, in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there are various great bodhisattvas such as Sūryagarbha, Candragarbha, Merugarbha, Gaganagañja, and Devagarbha, each of whom is named according to the object of their contemplation. For example, [as in the case of] observation...
The samādhi of entering the boundless void is named the "Treasury of Space" (*ākāśagarbha*). Now, this bodhisattva contemplates the suffering of the hells and gives rise to the bodhicitta;
having realized the secret treasury of the three virtues within the hell realm, he is able to rescue those suffering in the great hells of the ten directions, and is therefore named Kṣitigarbha.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, wishing to...
When he approaches, the assembly sees the great waters filling [the space]. When the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is about to arrive, the trichiliocosm suddenly becomes invisible.
When the Bodhisattva Candragarbha is about to arrive, a crescent moon appears above the heads of the entire assembly.
When the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha is about to arrive, wish-fulfilling jewels appear in the hands of each member of the gathering, raining down [precious things].

The jewel emits light, whereby one sees the lands of the ten directions and perceives that each respective element within one's own body becomes intensified; it becomes solid, heavy, and difficult to lift.

One should know that all things—the four great elements, space, mountains, oceans, sun, and moon, whether pertaining to the environment or its inhabitants—are none other than the single reality realm of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take any given phenomenon as their object of contemplation and thereby realize [this truth].
Having realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of this Dharma, one immediately realizes the true nature of all dharmas.
Therefore, all dharmas converge toward this Dharma; it is for this reason that this Dharma is called a "Treasury" (*piṭaka*). "Truly" (*satya*) means "reality.
"Reality" may be rendered as "accomplishment," and "accomplishment" means "fulfillment. The first inquiry concerning the Dharma is concluded. △ Second, the inquiry concerning the person, part one.
The second explanation of the doubt:

First, at that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Tathāgata, World-Honored One, Possessor of Unsurpassed Great Wisdom, for what reason do You not speak [it] Yourself, but instead desire to have the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha expound it?"
Fearing that the assembly might harbor doubts, [the text] acts on behalf of Dharmaratna to request the World-Honored One. It is by means of this that his true identity is revealed.
△ Second, the explanation of the answer, which has three parts: first, a general admonition; second, a detailed explanation; third, the concluding response. Now, the first part.
The Buddha told Jianjingxin: "Do not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority.
Sentient beings do not know that the fundamental and the manifested are not fixed; they will inevitably regard the Buddha as superior and the bodhisattvas as inferior.
These are all deluded conceptualizations and discriminations. Because of these discriminations, one does not enter the Dharma-gate of firm faith; therefore, it is entrusted to Jianjing."

Faith serves as the compass for all. △ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, directly clarifying the high rank of the stage; second, concurrently clarifying the excellence of the conditions. Now, the first:
Since this good man first resolved his mind, he has passed through immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
For kalpas past, he has already been able to cross the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and is fully perfected in merit;
yet, by the power of his sovereign original vows, he manifests through skillful means and transformations, appearing as reflections throughout the ten directions.
That he has resolved his mind [for enlightenment] after the passing of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas clarifies that his original cause is profound.

That he has fulfilled the merit of attaining *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) clarifies that his original fruit is sublime. That he manifests transformations through skillful means, appearing as reflections throughout the ten directions, clarifies that his manifested activity is vast and great.
△ Second, a concurrent clarification of the excellence of the conditions, which is further divided into two parts: first, the excellence of compassion; second, the excellence of vows.
First, regarding the excellence of his wisdom and eloquence:
although he universally traverses all buddha-fields and constantly performs meritorious deeds, his transformative influence is particularly profound in this world of five turbidities.
This is both because he is permeated by the power of his original vows and because of the karmic conditions of sentient beings who are ready to receive his transformation.
Furthermore, for eleven kalpas he has adorned this world and brought sentient beings to maturity;
therefore, within this assembly, his physical form is upright and majestic, and his majestic virtue is preeminent—none can surpass him except for the Tathāgata.
Moreover, regarding all the transformative activities in this world, with the sole exception of Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other great bodhisattvas, [he alone performs them].

They cannot equal it. By the power of this Bodhisattva’s original vow, he swiftly fulfills all the requests of sentient beings, can extinguish all their grave offenses, removes all obstacles, and brings them peace and security in the present life.

Although one may hold a high station, it is still necessary to cultivate through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). Although there is the cultivation of aspiration, one must also possess the karma to be transformed.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Among the classes of sentient beings, from beginningless time, their spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) are naturally and mutually interconnected;
many may belong to one, or one may belong to many. Therefore, those beings to be transformed are either common or uncommon. [The passage ends with "not..."]
Indeed, for many Buddhas to remain long in the world and each undergo such arduous toil would be truly of no benefit.
Since one Buddha alone can benefit all living beings, you should know that while a Buddha is able to deliver all sentient beings, he ultimately cannot deliver those who lack the karmic affinity;
this is not a false statement. He universally traverses all buddha-fields and constantly performs meritorious deeds. This is...
It is by virtue of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) that he does not abandon any being; yet, his transformative benefit is particularly profound within the five turbidities of this evil world.

This is the great compassion of same essence (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*), which especially pities those who are stubborn and defiant. It is permeated by the power of his original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna-bala*):
namely, that he would realize bodhi only after all sentient beings have been saved, and would not attain perfect enlightenment so long as hell is not empty.
