These are the Three Jewels sustained by one's own mind. This mind is without beginning and without end; therefore, it is eternal. This mind is without division and without partition.

Therefore, it is pervasive. Because this mind is uninterrupted and without deficiency, it is complete. Because this mind extends vertically through all time and pervades horizontally across all space, being neither contained nor broken, it is present everywhere.

Since one’s own mind is thus eternally pervasive and omnipresent, and since all the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha take this very mind as their essence, they too are essentially eternal, pervasive, and omnipresent.
It is not brought about by recollection; rather, it is through recollection that one clearly perceives it. △ Second, realizing the nature of the capacity for offering:
may these incense and flowers be made identical to the *dharmatā*, universally perfuming all Buddha-fields, and performing [their function].
Regarding Buddhist practice:
these very single incense sticks and single flowers originally manifest from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) according to conditions.

They each possess the complete functional capacity of the *dharmatā* in its entirety; they are not merely partial, for the *dharmatā* is fundamentally without divisions or portions and cannot be partitioned.

Because it is divided and partitioned. If one knows that incense and flowers are fundamentally identical in essence to the *dharmatā*, then they must likewise be identical in function to the *dharmatā*.
Thus, they can universally permeate all Buddha-fields to make offerings to the Triple Gem above, and furthermore perform Buddha-works to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings below.
Although this nature is inherently so, it must nonetheless rely upon the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

Only then is the merit of being in accord with the nature (dharmatā) fully realized. This concludes the initial general contemplation in accord with the nature. △ Second, regarding the specific contemplation of objects:

although one has already been able to contemplate each incense and each flower as being all-pervasive in accord with the nature, because the King of Vows is inexhaustible and the mind knows no satiety, it is necessary to separately and individually contemplate all offering implements and all sentient beings; furthermore, one must...
The distinct perceptions that constitute the body of the offerer and the Three Jewels who are the objects of offering are each mutually pervasive and inexhaustible;

through these ever-receding layers of inexhaustibility, one enters the ocean-like gateway of Samantabhadra’s vast method of offering. The text is divided into three parts: first, the pervasiveness of the mental offerings;
second, the pervasiveness of the body of the offerer; and third, the pervasiveness of the Three Jewels who are the objects of offering. First:
Furthermore, regarding the first of the two [aspects], the universal application of offering implements:
one should contemplate that at all times, all manner of offering implements exist throughout the ten directions. One should now think:
"I shall now employ all the various kinds of incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, flags, precious canopies, exquisite ornaments, and diverse musical instruments found throughout the ten directions."
Lamps, candles, and fires; food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; even including every variety of ornamental article for worship throughout the entirety of the ten directions.
Question: The offering implements of the ten directions each have their respective owners. If they are actually used, would one not be committing the offense of theft?

If they are not actually used, how can they be called "offerings"? Answer: If we refer to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), then the offering implements of the ten directions are all objects manifested within the single thought-moment of my own mind.
If we refer to the Consciousness-Only (Weishi) school, they are the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) upon the eighth consciousness.
The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the vessel-world transformed by the seeds of consciousness now takes as its object the objective aspect of one's own consciousness.

How, then, can this be called "stealing"? To practice offerings while thus realizing that all is representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is precisely what is called the true Dharma-offering; how could it be called unreal?
If one relies on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then even if one were to diligently offer incense and flowers held in hand, would there truly be [any substance to the act]?
Is this not practical? Now, if one contemplates the five heinous crimes in the mind, even without moving the body or speaking with the mouth, there will nonetheless be sin.

If one contemplates making offerings in the mind, even without burning incense or scattering flowers, how could there not be merit? How much more so when one employs the ritual implements of the ten directions within a single thought-moment;
this can immediately shatter the two attachments to self and dharmas, manifesting the compassion of the same essence. Furthermore...

This is not merely a matter of deluded feelings or empty imaginings; one must contemplate it and cultivate it. △ Second, the visualization of universal equality with all sentient beings, which has three parts:
first, visualizing the offering of equality; second, mindfulness of sympathetic joy; third, the vow for guidance. Now, the first part.
Recalling and mentally envisioning [the offerings], one universally offers them together with all sentient beings as an act of worship.
△ Second, the mindfulness of sympathetic joy:
One constantly reflects that within all worlds there are those who practice making offerings, and thinks, "I now rejoice in this."
△ Third, the vow to provide guidance:
If there are those who have not yet practiced making offerings, may they be guided so that they may practice making offerings.

May we universally join in presenting these offerings, thereby encompassing all present beings. Having rejoiced in those who have already practiced making offerings, may this likewise encompass all those of the past.

Go forth! To guide those who have not yet practiced making offerings, one should pervade all of the future—meaning that mindfulness continues in succession without interruption, such that the activities of body, speech, and mind never grow weary or exhausted. This concludes the first section: the pervasiveness of the initial thought-moment of offering.
Two: The vow for the pervasiveness of the physical body as the object of offering.
Furthermore, may my body swiftly reach all buddha-fields, and at each site of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, may I,
together with all sentient beings, offer up every kind of adorned article of worship.
Ordinary beings delusively identify the four great elements as the characteristics of their own bodies; thus they are restricted and cannot be pervasive.
Those of the Two Vehicles falsely calculate that things are impermanent, selfless, impure, suffering, and empty; thus they incline toward quiescence and have nothing by which to be pervasive.

Now, one directly contemplates that the nature of the body is itself the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because the nature of phenomena is pervasive, the body likewise follows along in its pervasiveness. As for this single body—
Regarding the offerings one contemplates and the sentient beings with whom one shares them, these have already been established as vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive;
how much more so for inexhaustible bodies, each using inexhaustible articles of offering, collectively and equally presenting them as offerings to all inexhaustible sentient beings.
In that case, would it not be without confusion and without obstruction? △ Third, the pervasiveness of the Three Jewels to whom offerings are made:
making offerings to the Dharma-body and Form-body of all Buddhas, to their śarīra relics, images, stūpas, temples, and pagodas, and to all Buddhist activities;
making offerings to all treasuries of the Dharma and all places where the Dharma is preached; and making offerings to all worthy and holy ones (*ārya*).

O Sangha. The Dharma-body is the principle realized; the Form-body is the reward of self-enjoyment, possessing inconceivable and subtle form and mind—namely, the ultimate and eternally abiding five aggregates. By mentioning "form," "mind" is implied therein. [End of] Chapter.

"Benefit" refers to the sacred relics (*śarīra*) left behind by the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Images" refers to those that emulate the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of that transformation body.
"Stūpas, temples, and all Buddhist rites" refers to the adornment of those relics and images.

If one realizes that phenomena arising through causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way, then each and every relic and image is [the embodiment of] the three [truths].
The body remains as it was, with the four virtues undiminished; how much more so for the form-body and the dharma-body! The same may be known regarding the Dharma and the Sangha.

Indeed, when one cultivates contemplation in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), even a single incense stick or a single flower is sufficient to universally make offerings to the Triple Gem;
how much more so when using all the offering implements existing throughout the ten directions? How much more so when further rejoicing in and guiding all sentient beings?

If all [beings] cultivate offerings in this way, how much more so for my own body, which reaches every single buddha-field, wherein each individual offering is used to universally make offerings to all the Triple Gem;
this may be called "layer upon layer without end, and endless layers. The first section, on the contemplation of cultivating offerings, is concluded.
II. The Contemplation of Benefiting Others, which subsumes the previous two types of offerings—general and specific—and dedicates them.
This brings about two kinds of adornment. Furthermore, of these two, the first vow accomplishes the adornment of merit, while the second vow accomplishes the adornment of wisdom.
Thus, the two types of cultivation arising from the fundamental nature are in turn used to adorn that single nature.
Now, for the first [vow]:
May I, together with all sentient beings, having practiced such offerings, gradually achieve the six pāramitās and the four immeasurable minds.
By relinquishing all that one possesses, one accomplishes generosity; by being pure and untainted, one accomplishes ethical discipline; and by having a mind free from anger...

Being free from vexation, one accomplishes patience (*kṣānti*). Being free from all indolence, one accomplishes vigor (*vīrya*). Being free from the defilement of distraction, one accomplishes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Being free from all obscurations, one accomplishes wisdom (*prajñā*). Causing others to obtain happiness constitutes the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).
To cause others to be free from suffering is the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*). To rejoice in others attaining happiness is the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*).
To maintain a mind that is always impartial, without distinction between enemy and friend, is the immeasurable of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa*).

By practicing even a single offering according to these, one is able to accomplish these ten dharma-gates and spontaneously and perfectly encompass all merits of the two benefits for self and others. △ Second, the vow to perfect the adornment of wisdom.
Yan deeply realized that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, of a single flavor and equality, pure and free from conceptual thought,
and ultimately perfect and complete.
Primordially quiescent, without arising or ceasing, and of a single equal flavor—this refers to all phenomena as the Middle Way, which is the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Free from conceptualization and pure—this refers to all phenomena as emptiness, which is the Knowledge of All (sarvajñatā).

Ultimately complete and perfect—this refers to all phenomena as the provisional, which is the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā). Thus, one deeply understands the three knowledges within a single mind.
All dharmas are none other than the three truths; awakening oneself and awakening others do not transcend this wondrous contemplation.
Second, the extensive cultivation of offerings is concluded. △ Third, the specific offering of calling the names.
Furthermore, you should separately focus your mind once more to make offerings to me, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
You should do so by reciting his name aloud, or if you prefer, by silent recitation; with single-minded devotion, address him thus: "Namo Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Recite his name in this manner until you have completed one thousand times.
Although one has already made universal offerings to the Triple Gem, I, Kṣitigarbha, am specifically the master who resolves the doubts of practitioners;

therefore, one should fix the mind upon me and offer special worship. As for the requirement to recite my name up to a thousand times, it is to cause roots of goodness to accumulate so as to perfect the conditions for resonance between the practitioner and the response;
it also symbolizes that a single thought-moment encompasses a thousand dharmas. △ Fourth, the Sincere Petition.
Having completed one thousand recitations, he spoke these words: "O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, endowed with great kindness and great compassion,
I pray that you will protect and keep mindful of me and all sentient beings, swiftly eliminating all obstacles and increasing pure faith,
so that what I now contemplate may accord with reality."
Although one may personally resolve one's own doubts, it is essential to state that this applies to all sentient beings;
only by keeping sentient beings in mind at every thought can one truly invoke the great compassion of the Bodhisattva. △ Fifth, the actual act of casting the wheel.
Having spoken these words, he then took a wooden wheel in his hand and cast it sideways upon a clean surface.
This concludes the first section, clarifying the method for divination by oneself according to the ritual. △ Second, clarifying the application of this method to others.
Thus, one who wishes to observe their own phenomena, or wishes to observe those of others, should know that it is exactly the same in all cases.
For a beginner who does not yet know their past lives, they must observe themselves to resolve doubts and regrets.

Since they have not yet attained the path-eye of knowing the minds of others, even when wishing to observe others, they must likewise rely on the five aforementioned methods. △ Third, the explanation of divination.
Examine in detail; whether observing oneself or others, one must likewise investigate with such scrutiny. Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, clarifying what appears; second, clarifying what does not appear. Regarding the first:

as for examining the marks of the wheel (*cakra*), one should thoroughly observe, contemplate, and verify each and every karmic manifestation as it appears, whether it be purely complete or otherwise.

The ten wholesome actions; or those who possess all ten unwholesome actions; or those whose wholesome and unwholesome deeds are intermingled; or those who possess wholesome deeds but not all of them; or those who possess unwholesome deeds but not all of them.
Such karmic causes differ in their types, and their habitual tendencies and retributions are each distinct, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has explained extensively elsewhere.
One should recollect, contemplate, and observe the manifested seeds of karma in relation to the present.

Regarding the various matters of suffering, pleasure, auspiciousness, and misfortune experienced as the fruits of worldly retribution, as well as those acquired through the habits of afflictions and karma:
when these correspond [to one's state], it is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*). If they do not correspond, it is said that one has not been sincere; this is termed "falsehood" (*vibhrama*).
The karmic seeds manifested [in dreams] refer to those things manifested upon the wheel, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.

They are termed "corresponding" only when they accord with the retributions of the present life, or accord with the habitual tendencies of afflictions and karma; otherwise, they are termed "erroneous" due to a lack of sincere intent.
For example, if one manifests not killing, it should correspond to being currently free from illness and possessing a long life, or perhaps manifesting compassion.
Regarding the mind: if one does not currently steal, one should now lack nothing; or else, one should always be content, and so forth.

Again, as with current killing, one should now have much illness and much affliction; or else, one should constantly harbor murderous intent. If, moreover, one currently steals, one should now have little wealth;

or else, one should constantly suffer loss and deprivation, or constantly harbor a thieving mind, and so forth. One must reflect upon and verify each of these for oneself; it is not otherwise possible.
This concludes the full exposition. △ Second, explaining what does not appear, which has two parts: first, when both do not appear; second, when some things do not appear.
Regarding the first:
if, when examining the marks of the wheels, neither good nor evil karma appears, this person has already realized the mind of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Devoted solely to seeking liberation, they no longer delight in receiving worldly retributions.
All tainted karmas gradually become feeble and cease to increase; therefore, they do not manifest.

The untainted wisdom-mind refers to the eight patiences and eight knowledges of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), which pertain generally to the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and specifically to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

At the stage of the first faith (*prathama-śraddhā*), one has already severed the seeds of the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of the three realms and no longer creates karma that invites future existence (*punarbhava*).

Even if there are previously perfumed karmic seeds, they gradually become weakened and do not increase. Alternatively, at the stage of the five circular grades (*pañca-parivarta*), one circularly suppresses the afflictions.
Affliction. One should abandon co-residence in the defiled land and be born in the pure land of co-residence.

Although one has not yet realized untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), both good and evil may fail to manifest because the power of perfect contemplation is so strong. △ Second, that which does not manifest.

Furthermore, regarding those who possess neither pure goodness nor pure evil: for these two types of persons, whatever karmic actions of good or evil do not manifest are all weak and unable to draw forth their results; therefore, they do not manifest.
When the seeds of virtuous karma are strong, they can bring about a pleasant ripening (*vipāka*); when the seeds of non-virtuous karma are strong, they can bring about a painful ripening.
If the seeds are weak, they still require moisture to act; they do not immediately draw forth their fruit, and thus they do not manifest.
By this principle, it is clear that the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states—obscured and unobscured—are not termed virtuous or non-virtuous. Second, a detailed explanation of divination.
The Dharma is concluded. △ Third, the admonition and exhortation for future generations:

If the disciples of the Buddha in future ages have already divined that their good and evil karmic retributions correspond [to their actions], and when they encounter objects of the five desires to their heart's content, they must not indulge themselves to give rise to negligence (this is the admonition). They should instead reflect as follows:
"Because of such virtuous karma from my past lives, I have now obtained this retribution. I should now further advance in my cultivation and must not cease.
(This is an exhortation. If one encounters various calamities, manifold afflictions, and inauspicious events;

if one is beset by confusion and fear, or when things do not accord with one's wishes—one should accept these with equanimity, without allowing for doubt or regret that would cause one to withdraw from cultivating wholesome karma. (This is an admonition. Thus..."
One should reflect thus: "It is solely because I committed such evil karma in my past lives that I now receive this retribution.
I must now repent for that evil karma, diligently practice its antidote, and cultivate other virtues.
I must not remain in indolence or negligence, nor allow the various masses of suffering to further accumulate. This is called the method for observing the signs of the first wheel.

Within this, there are two successive exhortations. The first is for those whose wishes have been fulfilled: it admonishes them not to be negligent and encourages them to advance further in their practice.
The second is for those whose wishes have not been fulfilled: it admonishes them not to retreat or regret, and encourages them to cultivate all manner of virtues.

The first section, showing the characteristics of the first wheel, is concluded. △ Second, showing the characteristics of the second wheel, in three parts: first, the direct presentation of the wheel’s characteristics;

second, a detailed presentation of the method of divination; third, a specific explanation of the method of repentance. Regarding the first [of these three], there are three parts: first, showing the characteristics; second, showing the meaning; third, the functional efficacy. Now, the first [part].

"Good son, if you wish to examine and discern the past karma accumulated over long or short periods, its strength or weakness, and its various distinctions of magnitude, you should again carve wood into three wheels.
Let each of the body, speech, and mind preside over one wheel, and record them by inscribing characters upon them.
Furthermore, on one side of the center of each wheel, draw a single line that is thick and long, extending right to the edge. Next..."
On the second side, draw a single line that is fine and short, ensuring it does not reach the edge.
Next, on the third side, make a single horizontal incision like a line, making it coarse and deep. Finally, on the fourth side, also make a horizontal incision, making it fine and shallow.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning:
One should know that virtuous karma is like decorative painting, while non-virtuous karma is like damage and carving.

When a painting is large and expansive, it demonstrates that one has accumulated virtue for a long time, that one’s karmic activities have been intense, and that one’s deeds have been preeminent. When the painting is fine...
Those that are short indicate that one has approached [the path] through the accumulation of merit; their initial training was based on dull faculties, and what they have practiced is slight.

Those whose incisions are coarse and deep indicate that one has long practiced evil; their actions have been predominant, and the remaining retribution is likewise heavy. Those whose incisions are fine and shallow—[indicate... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)

This indicates that one who has regressed from wholesome states and is close to beginning to practice unwholesome dharmas has not yet reached the point where their committed karma becomes predominant;
or, even if they have generated grave evil, they have already repented—this is what is called "minor evil."

Great virtue, small virtue, and great non-virtue each have two meanings. Regarding the two meanings of great virtue: first, it may be accumulated over a long duration; second, it may be intense and predominant.
Regarding the two meanings of small virtue: first, it may not have lasted long; second, the action performed may be slight.
There are two types of great evil: first, that which has accumulated over a long period; second, that which has increased in intensity through its performance.

There are three meanings regarding small evil: first, that which has not yet persisted for long; second, that which has not yet reached a state of increase; third, that which has already been repented of, thereby transforming what was heavy into what is light.
Great goodness and great evil can result in results experienced either in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) or in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*). Small goodness and small [evil]...

Evil karma that was to be experienced in subsequent lives may be moistened so that it becomes karma to be experienced in the next life, or it may be diminished so that it becomes karma of indefinite timing.
That which does not appear within the marks of the first wheel is karma of indefinite timing.
Furthermore, whenever untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises, all seeds of karma to be experienced in the next life or in subsequent lives can be destroyed; this excludes only—
Karma to be experienced in the present life has not yet been entirely extinguished; furthermore, it can be transformed from heavy to light. △ Third, the functional capacity:

"Good son, if one examines the marks of the first wheel, one may know the distinctions between the good and evil karma created in past lives, but one cannot know the duration of their accumulation, nor the strength, weakness, magnitude, or smallness of the karma performed. For this reason, one must..."
[This section] concerns the divination of the second wheel-sign.

The initial direct demonstration of the wheel-signs is concluded. △ Second, the detailed demonstration of the method of divination has two parts: first, explaining the divination; second, explaining the examination.
Now, the first [part].
If one divines by means of the signs of the second wheel, one should rely upon the karma manifested within the signs of the first wheel.
If it pertains to the body, cast the sign of the body wheel; if it pertains to speech, cast the sign of the speech wheel; if it pertains to the mind, cast the sign of the mind wheel.
One must not attempt to divine all three simultaneously with a single casting; rather, one should focus on the primary object of inquiry.
First, regarding good and evil: cast the divination separately according to the wheel to which each belongs.

For every instance of good and evil, one must perform a separate divination based on the primary thought. This is like the good and evil of the body; if three [types] manifest, they must be treated accordingly.
In that case, one must cast [the divination sticks] separately three times for the mouth, four times for the body, and three times for the mind; all are treated in this same manner.
As for those that do not manifest, there is no need to cast them. △ Second, the examination.

Furthermore, if in the examination of the first wheel-sign one obtains only bodily goodness, yet in this second wheel-sign one obtains bodily evil—this means there was no sincerity and the signs were not in accord;
it is called "false and erroneous. Moreover, regarding lack of correspondence:
if in the examination of the first wheel-sign one obtains the karma of non-killing and the karma of stealing, with the mind being the primary factor...
Regarding the observation of the non-killing karma, if one obtains bodily evil within the second wheel-sign, it is called "incompatible.

Furthermore, if one observes that from birth until the present one has not delighted in the karma of killing and has committed no sinful act of killing, yet the mind primarily intends to observe the karma of killing, and if within this second wheel-sign one obtains great bodily evil, this is called "non-... [incompatible].
Correspondence. The principle that the remaining karmas of speech and mind are non-correspondent should likewise be understood.
The second section, detailing the methods of divination, is concluded. △ Third, the specific explanation of the methods of repentance has three parts:
first, explaining that one should practice repentance; second, correctly demonstrating the method of repentance; third, clarifying the signs of attaining purity. Now, the first part.
"Good son, if there are sentient beings in future ages who wish to seek liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
and who first resolve their minds to learn and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*),

they should first observe the amount and the gravity of the evil karma they have committed in past lives. If their evil karma is great and heavy, they must not immediately study meditative concentration."
Wisdom. One should first practice the method of repentance. Why is this?

Because this person’s habitual evil mind from past lives is so fierce and sharp, they will inevitably commit many evils in the present, violating the heavy prohibitions. Because they have violated these heavy prohibitions...
If one practices meditative concentration and wisdom without first repenting to bring oneself to purity, there will be many obstacles and one will be unable to achieve success.
One may suffer from loss of mind or mental derangement, be afflicted by external malevolent forces, or accept false teachings that increase evil views.
Therefore, one should first practice the method of repentance. If the root of one's precepts is pure, as well as [the purification of] past lives...
When one's transgressions become slight, one is then freed from all hindrances.

Although the nature of karma is empty, its retribution is not lost; therefore, one must cultivate the power of repentance through habitual practice to cause those evil seeds to gradually weaken and no longer increase, so that one may then be fit to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom without encountering perverse thoughts.

...and so forth. △ Second, the actual exposition of the method of repentance, in two parts: first, clarifying the ritual procedure for repentance; second, clarifying the duration of the repentance period. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, extensively clarifying the Buddhist services during the day; second, briefly indicating the Buddhist services at night. In the first of these, there are nine points in total:
first, clarifying the purification of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*); second, clarifying offerings of incense and flowers; third, clarifying purity; [and so on].
The fourth section clarifies the invocation of names and prostrations; the fifth explains the confession of transgressions; the sixth clarifies the making of exhortations and aspirations;
the seventh clarifies the making of aspirations for sympathetic joy; the eighth clarifies the making of aspirations for dedication; and the ninth clarifies the recitation of names.

To examine these in detail, they comprise various ritual methods such as those found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vaipulya* sūtras, the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*.

All [previous versions] were established by the Four Great Reliant Masters (Catur-āśraya-mahāsattva) who, relying upon the scriptural texts, interpreted the underlying intent and deliberated before establishing the ten categories (*daśa-varga*).
None, however, was as clear and manifest as this sutra, requiring no further deliberation—save for the single category of the "Initial Petition" (*pūrvakāla-adhyeṣaṇā*).
Having previously burned incense to offer earnest prayers and drawn lots for divine guidance, I have now ventured to add this vow.
I dare not offer a single word of forced interpretation. First, clarify and purify the place of practice.

Good son, one who wishes to cultivate the method of repentance should dwell in a quiet location and, according to their capacity, adorn a single room, placing Buddhist ritual objects within it, installing the scriptures and Dharma, and hanging silk banners and canopies.
Regarding the ritual procedures for the maṇḍalas of the Secret Mantra section, they should be made as exquisitely adorned as possible;

however, what is stated here is merely according to one's capacity, intended specifically for those in the degenerate age who lack supportive conditions. As for "Buddhist objects," this refers to images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whether fashioned by modeling or painting—any of these are permissible.
As for "the sūtras and Dharma," this refers to this very sūtra, or otherwise any other Jewel of the Mahāyāna Dharma; these too are acceptable.
It is not permissible [to do so]. One may hang silk banners and canopies as adornments, whether made of brocade, plain silk, or even paper and calico;
these may all be provided according to one's means. △ Second, explaining the offering of incense and flowers.
One should seek and gather incense and flowers to cultivate offerings.
Following other ritual procedures, one must burn incense and scatter flowers at every session, in accordance with the visualization methods explained previously.
This [section] follows the order of the text and is therefore placed second; however, according to the sequence of practice, it must certainly follow after the purification of the three karmas.
△ Purify the three karmas through the three types of clarity.
Bathe the body and wash clothes so that they do not become foul or filthy.
This is also like other rules of conduct: whenever one defecates, one must change clothes and bathe. Having finished bathing, put on clean [clothes].
Only when the robes are purified may one enter the maṇḍala to practice the Way. △ Fourth, the explanation of invoking the names and paying homage:

During the daytime, while remaining within this inner chamber, one should invoke the names and single-mindedly pay homage three times daily to the seven Buddhas of the past and the fifty-three Buddhas.
Subsequently, facing each of the ten directions one by one, one should mentally direct one's thoughts toward all Buddhas everywhere and pay homage to them in their entirety.
One should pay homage to all the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas, their *śarīra* relics, images, stupas, temples, and all other Buddha-activities.

Next, one should again universally pay homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Furthermore, one should direct the mind to universally pay homage to all Dharma-treasuries throughout the ten directions.

Then, one should direct the mind to universally pay homage to all worthy ones (*ārya*) and sages (*ārya-pudgala*) throughout the ten directions. Only thereafter should one specifically call out their names.
I pay homage to me, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
△ Fifth, explaining the confession of transgressions:
Having thus paid homage, one should speak of the transgressions committed, addressing [the Buddhas] with single-minded devotion: "I only pray that the Great [Buddhas] of the ten directions..."
O Compassionate Honored One, bear witness to me and protect me with mindfulness. I now repent; I shall not create such offenses again.

May I and all sentient beings swiftly eliminate the immeasurable kalpas of transgressions—the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, perversity, slandering and disparaging the Triple Gem, and the sins of icchantikas.
Furthermore, one should reflect that the nature of these offenses arises solely from a deluded and inverted mind.

Arise! There is nothing fixed or substantial to be found; from the beginning, it is only empty and quiescent. May all sentient beings swiftly reach the fundamental source of the mind and forever extinguish the roots of transgression.
One must confess all misdeeds committed, namely, all evil karma created in this present life, or the great evils manifested within the wheel-sign;
these must all be openly disclosed and laid bare. This pertains to the ten mental states for reversing the flow of saṃsāra.
From three types of mind, five types of mind arise; together with the subsequent exhortations, rejoicings, and so forth, these collectively constitute the ten minds.
Because of the first, which is deep faith in cause and effect; the second, which gives rise to great shame and remorse;

and the third, which gives rise to great dread—therefore, one now declares the transgressions committed, which is the fourth: the confession and repentance (*pratideśanā*). No longer [will they be committed].
To perform this is the fifth [step]: severing the continuity of the mind.

To vow, "May I and all sentient beings swiftly attain the eradication of the ten non-virtues, the four grave offenses, and so forth," is the sixth: generating the bodhicitta. And the seventh is overturning one's past heavy transgressions.
The contemplation on the nature of sin and so forth corresponds to the tenth [stage], "Now Knowing Emptiness and Quiescence. The exhortation in the subsequent text corresponds to the ninth.

The recollection of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the sympathetic joy correspond to the eighth, "Sympathetic Joy in All Merits. The dedication of merit also encompasses the meanings of the sixth, seventh, and tenth stages.
Regarding past evil karma, if one discusses its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), it has already ceased in a single moment.
Although [the afflictions] have been extinguished, the seeds that were perfumed remain hidden within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Due to the power of the self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, these seeds are nurtured and reinforced moment by moment, allowing them to increase. This present act of confession is precisely the vanguard for destroying self-grasping.
It is like the seeds of plants and trees hidden beneath the earth; they will inevitably sprout stems and leaves. Now that they have been unearthed...

If they are exposed, they will naturally be destroyed. Furthermore, even if old seeds have been exposed, if their continuity is not permanently severed, then newly perfumed seeds will be able to mutually reinforce the old seeds, growing and flourishing in succession without end.
Therefore, one must vow never to create them again. Moreover, due to self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), one falsely discriminates between self and others; whatever is thus produced—

There is no sentient being who shares the same substance as oneself that is not harmed or afflicted by one's offenses; it is like two hands within a single body wounding each other, whereby one personally encounters suffering.
Now, having shattered the false attachment to a self, one universally eliminates the various offenses of all sentient beings on their behalf;
this is by no means like a deer leaping alone. Furthermore, the nature of these offenses arises solely from a deluded and inverted mind, and not...
Throughout the internal, external, and intermediate locations, that which has passed away is already extinguished; that which is present does not abide; and that which is yet to come does not exist.
If one carefully investigates the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is nothing determinate or substantial to be found.

It is like the flowers in the sky seen by one with cataracts: the essence of those flowers is fundamentally only empty and quiescent. Failing to realize this fundamental emptiness, one increases [the perception of] non-existence.

Regarding the cataract of ignorance: if one contemplates and realizes in every thought that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, no longer staring with wide eyes to discriminate illusory flowers, then the disease of the cataract will gradually be removed and the flowers will likewise gradually diminish, until the fatigue of the eyes has ceased and the appearance of the flowers vanishes of its own accord.

Therefore, it is said: "One swiftly reaches the root of the mind and eternally extinguishes the source of transgressions. To contemplate the emptiness of the nature of transgressions is called the Repentance of True Reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is its name.

The Repentance of Non-arising is also called the Great Adornment Repentance; it consists of the contemplation of mind-only consciousness and the contemplation of the reality of True Suchness (tathatā).
One must not fail to understand this. △ Sixth, explaining the arousal of the vow of exhortation.
Next, one should further give rise to the vow of exhortation: "I pray that all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment may swiftly attain it;
and those who have already attained perfect enlightenment, I pray that they remain forever in the world, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma and not entering parinirvāṇa."

Because it exhorts [the Buddha] to eliminate demonic obstacles, it is also called "repentance. The Māra Pāpīyān constantly seeks to obstruct Bodhisattvas while they sit at the site of enlightenment so that they may not attain Buddhahood;
whenever the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, he constantly seeks to incite his heart toward destruction;
and he also repeatedly requests the Buddha to enter parinirvāṇa swiftly. Now, one exhorts him to attain enlightenment and exhorts him to dwell long in the world.
"Exhorting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma" refers to overturning and destroying those three kinds of evil. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*):
the Bodhisattva represents the various wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*) of one's own mind, while Māra represents the various unwholesome mental factors of one's own mind.

Now, causing these wholesome mental factors to be associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is called "swiftly attaining perfect enlightenment. This occurs moment by moment, always without interruption.
This is called "abiding eternally without extinction. To transform other minds and mental factors is called "turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
△ Seventh, clarifying the aspiration for sympathetic joy:
Next, one should further give rise to the aspiration of sympathetic joy, vowing that I and all sentient beings shall ultimately and forever abandon envy.
With a mind free from envy, one rejoices in all the merits of study and all that has been accomplished by everyone throughout all buddha-fields across the three periods of time.
Rejoicing in this eliminates the obstacle of jealousy; therefore, it is also called "repentance.
All Buddhas, the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, and the ordinary beings of the Six Realms are all, within the single thought-moment of my present mind, of one and the same essence.

Fundamentally, there is no distinction between self and other. It is due to the grasping of a self that one falsely discriminates between self and others, giving rise to jealousy. Now, I repent of this fault deeply.
To give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward all ordinary beings and sages with equanimity is to take up the goodness of the Dharma-realm as one’s own goodness;
such goodness is truly great. Why must one necessarily move one's own mind, body, and speech to perform virtuous deeds?
We see that when another carries a lamp, we too receive its light; when another burns incense, we too are perfumed by it.
The roots of goodness of the same essence are as clear as this. How is it that, obstructed by ignorance, you do not know how to receive and sustain them, but instead give rise to jealousy?
If you can rejoice [in others' merit], you will know that the roots of goodness cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are fundamentally shared with all sentient beings;
you originally possess a share in them, which does not require forceful seeking. Thus, the *Great Buddha-Topknot Sūtra* says:
All the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are entirely bestowed upon this person. They shall always be born in the same place as all Buddhas.
Their immeasurable merits will be like a cluster of akṣa fruits, cultivated together in one place and never to be dispersed. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If a bodhisattva knows that all the merits of the Buddhas are their own merits, this is [the mark of a true bodhisattva]."
This is a most extraordinary teaching. Furthermore, a sutra states: "One shares the same treasury of roots of goodness as all bodhisattvas.

Moreover, the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* says: "The practitioner should know that the merits performed by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, noble ones of the two vehicles, ordinary beings, humans, and devas are all one's own merits; therefore, one should rejoice in them accordingly. Alas!
One may thereby attain awakening. △ Eighth, clarifying the vow of dedication:

Next, one should again make the vow of dedication: "May all the merits I have cultivated benefit all sentient beings, so that they may together proceed toward Buddha-wisdom and reach the city of Nirvana."

Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) can extinguish the obstacles of attachment to the three realms of existence; thus it is also called "repentance" (*kaukṛtya*). It benefits all: it is the dedication of oneself toward others;
it is the dedication toward the same goal of Buddha-wisdom; it is the dedication of causes toward the fruit; and it is the arrival at the city of Nirvāṇa.

This is the dedication of phenomena toward principle. Dedication of phenomena toward principle is called the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*); dedication of causes toward the fruit is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*). Dedication...
Turning toward others is called the Mahayana mind. The direct mind manifests the Dharmakaya of severed virtues; the profound mind accomplishes the Prajna of wisdom-virtues;
and the Mahayana mind accomplishes the liberation of benevolent virtues. Practice arises entirely from nature, and practice is entirely within nature;
from beginning to end, one never departs from the Secret Treasury. △ Ninth, clarifying the invocation of the Name.
Having thus made this vow of dedication, one should again go to another quiet room and sit upright with a single-minded focus.

One should either recite or silently contemplate my name, reducing sleep as much as possible. If drowsiness and mental obscuration are excessive, one should circumambulate within the sanctuary while reciting and contemplating.

As for those who merely single-mindedly recite and silently contemplate the Name, this is precisely because their evil karma is so heavy that they cannot immediately cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Nevertheless, whether sitting or walking, if one single-mindedly recites and contemplates it, this is itself the true skillful means (*upāya*) of meditative concentration and wisdom.
This is because the vast and majestic name of my Guṇa-Parvata (Earth-Treasury) summons the fruition [of Buddhahood].
The supreme true merit is able to act as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings, causing them to extinguish sins and eliminate obstacles in every moment of thought.
As stated in both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra*,
the merit of holding the names of sixty-two billion *Gaṅgā*-sands of Dharma-Princes is exactly equal to the merit of holding the name of Avalokiteśvara alone.
They are equal and without distinction. Furthermore, the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"Suppose there were a person who, for the duration of a hundred kalpas, with a sincere heart, took refuge in Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and their like."

To recite the name, perform prostrations, and make offerings while seeking various aspirations is not as effective as for someone who, for the duration of a single meal, with a sincere heart takes refuge in, recites the name of, pays homage to, and makes offerings to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha while seeking their various aspirations;
such a person will quickly have those aspirations fulfilled. Why is this? Because such a Great Being desires to bring all beings to spiritual maturity.
Because he is a sentient being who has long cultivated firm great vows and great compassion with courageous diligence, surpassing all other bodhisattvas;
therefore, you all should make offerings to him. This shall now be explained by way of two intentions. First, the intention of equality:
the dharma-nature realized by six billion two hundred million [beings] is equal to that realized by this one Great Being. One hundred...
The dharma-nature realized throughout kalpas is equal to that realized in the duration of a single meal. Regarding the second point, the distinction in their underlying intent:
the karmic conditions shared by the sentient beings of this land with sixty-two billion great bodhisattvas are not as profound as the karmic conditions shared with the Great Being Avalokiteśvara;
indeed, the karmic conditions shared with the Great Being Avalokiteśvara are the most profound of all.
Furthermore, the karmic conditions of the Great Being Kṣitigarbha are even more profound.
Moreover, as for the name that is invoked—whether it is understood or not—it is fundamentally the three truths within a single realm.

As for the thought that invokes it—whether it is realized or not—it is fundamentally the three contemplations within a single mind. Furthermore, although the name invoked is indeed the three truths, they remain distinct and clear.
This clarity is the inconceivable provisional (parikalpita). Although the mindfulness that can accord with it consists of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), it cannot be found when sought;

this is the inconceivable empty (śūnyatā). There is nothing external to the subject, and no subject external to the object; the simultaneous forgetting and simultaneous illumination of both is the inconceivable middle (madhyama).

Furthermore, it is called "name" because it exists due to mindfulness, and there is no name outside of mindfulness; this is precisely the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*).
The subject that contemplates and the object contemplated are, in their very essence, beyond all dependence; they are neither arising nor ceasing, eternally abiding within the one mind.
This is precisely the true contemplation of *tathatā*. Furthermore, this one mind is itself meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the act of reciting it is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although those at the stage of the "name" (*nāman*) in the Perfect Teaching have already understood that both the reciter and the recited are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they still possess [the obstructions] from beginningless time.
The power of karmic obstacles is strong; one must rely upon the Great Name as an object for fixing the mind, gradually causing the two hindrances of distraction and dullness to be removed.
This is precisely what is meant by "fixing the conditions upon the Dharma-realm" and "a single thought-moment of the Dharma-realm.

For a person of the Perfect Teaching who receives the Dharma, there is no dharma that is not perfect. How could one ever look down upon the practice of holding the Name as a provisional or shallow act? [End of] First Day, Morning Session.
At that time, the Buddha’s activities were concluded. △ Second, a brief indication of the Buddha’s activities during the night.

Next, when it reaches the period of night, if there are matters concerning lamps and candles for illumination, one should likewise respectfully make offerings, repent, and make vows during the three periods of the day.
If one is unable to provide for matters of illumination, one should simply remain in another quiet room.

If one can provide lamps and candles while single-mindedly reciting and mindful of [the Buddha], then one may practice the path at the same time and on the same day. If one cannot provide these, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Name.
This easy practice of skillful means was opened specifically for those who lack supporting conditions. Part One.
The ritual for the rite of repentance is hereby concluded. △ Second, clarifying the period of repentance:

Practice this method of repentance daily in this manner, ensuring it is not neglected or abandoned. If a person has possessed a foundation of goodness from distant past lives, [they shall attain success].

If one encounters adverse conditions for a time and commits unwholesome deeds, yet their karmic obstructions are slight, their mind is sharp and resolute, and their mental power is strong, they shall attain purity after seven days and be freed from all obstacles.
For such sentient beings, there are infinite distinctions in the thickness or thinness of their karma and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties; some may attain purity after fourteen days.
They become pure; or after three weeks, or even after seven weeks, they attain purity.
If there are various grave offenses that are particularly severe regarding both the past and the present, they attain purity after one hundred days.
It may take two hundred days, or even up to one thousand days, to attain purification.

However, for those of extremely dull faculties whose karmic obstructions are most heavy, they need only give rise to a courageous and resolute mind, disregarding concern for their own bodies or lives;

they should constantly and diligently recite [the name], circumambulate day and night, reduce sleep, perform prostrations and repentance, make vows, and joyfully cultivate offerings without indolence.
One must not abandon it, even at the cost of one’s life; one must never cease or retreat. With such diligence, one will surely attain purity within a thousand days.
If practicing alone, one should set the attainment of the signs of purity as the goal. If ten people observe the retreat together, they should practice during the six periods of day and night.

Thus, whether it be seven days, twenty-one days, or forty-nine days and so forth, there is nothing that would be improper; those of high intelligence can determine this for themselves. Part Two concludes the formal demonstration of the method of repentance.
△ Part Three: Clarifying the Signs of Attaining Purity. This has three sections: First, clarifying how the signs depend on the wheel of practice;

Second, clarifying that one attains results according to their prayers; Third, clarifying that the sincere mind is the cause. Within the first of these, there are three parts: First... [text continues].
First, the explicit explanation of the wheel upon which one relies, second, the simultaneous explanation of other characteristics, and third, the distinction from what is not the present [subject].

First: "Good son, if you wish to know the pure characteristics, starting from the time seven days have passed since you began your practice, you should, every day at dawn, place the second wheel-mark in your hand and cast it three times in succession."
If body, speech, and mind are all purely wholesome, this is called attaining purity.
It does not matter whether the goodness is great or small; provided that all three throws are wholesome and free from evil, it is immediately termed "purity.
△ Second, an ancillary clarification of other characteristics.

In this way, as for those future sentient beings who are able to practice repentance, although each of them has practiced virtue within the Buddha-dharma since the distant past, there are various differences in the thickness or thinness of their karma according to whichever merits they have cultivated.
Therefore, when they attain purification, their manifestations will also differ; some may...
When sentient beings attain the state where the three karmas are purely wholesome, they further obtain various other auspicious signs. Some sentient beings,
when attaining the wholesome signs of the three karmas, may, within a single day and night, again see light filling their room,
or hear an exceptionally sublime and wonderful fragrance, such that body and mind are refreshed and joyful, or they may have virtuous dreams, seeing the Buddha’s body coming to them.
To act as a witness, he stroked their heads with his hand and exclaimed, "Excellent! You are now pure; I come to bear witness for you.
Alternatively, they may see the body of a Bodhisattva coming in a dream to act as a witness, or they may see the form of a Buddha emitting light in a dream to act as a witness.
One truly attains the mark of the pure wheel and simultaneously experiences various spiritual responses; therefore, this is the manifestation of wholesome roots.
△ Third, distinguishing what is not [the case]:
If a person has not yet attained the auspicious signs of the three karmas, but merely first sees or hears such various matters, then it is false.
Deception, delusion, fraud, and falsehood are not auspicious signs.
The mark of the wheel is a single dharma established through the majestic spiritual power of the Great Being Kṣitigarbha; seek it according to the Dharma.

There is absolutely no error in this. Since one has not yet attained the signs of purity, any prior visions of light, smelling of fragrances, or obtaining extraordinary and auspicious dreams all belong to the activities of Māra;
one must not be deceived by them. This concludes the initial clarification of the basis through the wheel of dependence.

△ Second, explaining that what is sought is surely obtained. Part three: First, explaining the attainment of meditative concentration and wisdom; second, explaining the attainment of freedom from affliction; third, explaining the attainment of pure precepts.
Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts: first, explaining the manifest benefit; second, explaining the hidden benefit. Now, the first.

If there are those who have previously established a foundation for supramundane goodness and possess a sharp, powerful concentration of mind, at that time I manifest my body according to their needs for deliverance.
I radiate the great light of compassion to bring them peace and security, freeing them from all doubt and fear.
I may display various supernatural transformations through my miraculous powers, or cause them to remember the events and wholesome deeds they performed throughout their past lives.
Or, according to their inclinations, he may preach various profound and essential teachings for them.
That person will immediately attain resolute faith in the vehicle they have directed toward, or gradually realize and obtain the fruits of the śramaṇa path.
△ Second, clarifying the hidden benefit. Furthermore,
even if those sentient beings are not yet able to see my transformation body preaching the Dharma, if they simply study with a sincere mind and cause their body,
speech, and mind to attain the signs of purity, I shall likewise protect and keep them in mind, causing those sentient beings [to attain benefit].

Various obstacles will be swiftly extinguished; Māra Pāpīyān will not come to cause destruction, nor will any of the ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachers, external paths, or spirits and ghosts come to create disturbances.
All five hindrances will gradually diminish, enabling one to cultivate the various dhyānas and wisdom.

Whether one should receive benefit through manifest response or through hidden response, it arises entirely from the power of one’s own roots of goodness and from the Bodhisattva’s subtle wisdom that discerns the capacities of beings.
If you can believe this, then why doubt when you devote yourself single-mindedly to prostration and repentance?
This concludes the first section, clarifying the attainment of meditative concentration and wisdom. △ Second, clarifying the attainment of freedom from affliction.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings in future ages who, though not seeking the path of liberation through meditative concentration and wisdom,
nevertheless encounter various calamities, poverty, suffering, and are oppressed by grief and affliction,
one should likewise reverently pay homage to and make offerings to them, repent of their evil deeds, and constantly make vows at all times and in all places.
If one recites my name with a diligent mind and with utmost sincerity, they shall also swiftly be liberated from various forms of decline and affliction;
after casting off this life, they shall be reborn in a favorable realm.
Even if they do not resolve to transcend the world, they still cause them to obtain worldly benefits; that is to say, even the smallest blades of grass receive its moistening nourishment.
If one relies on the provisional teaching, this is for the sake of those who are icchantikas (those devoid of Buddha-nature) to preach the ten wholesome dharmas.
If one relies on the ultimate meaning, this is a gradual and skillful guidance that ultimately causes them to enter the Buddha-way step by step. △ Third, the explanation of the light.

Regarding the attainment of pure precepts, there are two further sections: first, clarifying how one who has committed grave offenses may repent and receive them; second, clarifying how one may receive them without a teacher.

Now, for the first: furthermore, in the future, if there are sentient beings—whether lay or ordained—who wish to receive the pure and wondrous precepts but have previously committed grave and excessive sins such that they are unable to receive them, they should likewise practice as described above.
Regarding the method of repentance: once they have been led to cultivate a sincere mind and attain the wholesome signs of body, speech, and mind, one may then accept [the precepts].

This applies whether they are laypeople who have violated four of the five lifelong precepts, or those who have violated four of the eight precepts for one day and night, or those who have violated the ten grave precepts of the Bodhisattva vows; or whether they are monastics who have violated the precepts of a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī.

The four grave offenses within the *śīla* (precepts), or the four grave offenses within the *śikṣamāṇā* discipline, or the four grave offenses within the *bhikṣu* and *bhikṣuṇī* precepts, are all termed "borderline offenses" (*antimā āpatti*).
As they are subsumed under the category of "grave obstacles," they are called "superior grave offenses."
If one follows the Vinaya Piṭaka, repentance is not permitted, and it is not possible to receive all the categories of precepts again.
If one follows the Brahmajāla Sūtra, one must take the appearance of auspicious signs as the deadline. Now, according to this sūtra, one takes the attainment of the pure wheel as the deadline.
Furthermore, the seven heinous offenses and others are also called "superior heavy sins"; even according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, they are not... [permitted].
He permitted them to receive the precepts. According to this sutra, if one attains the pure wheel-sign (*cakrāṅka*), one may then receive them;

this is truly an extraordinary and vast act of compassion. II. Clarifying that one may receive them even without a teacher, which has two parts: first, clarifying the Bodhisattva’s three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara*);
second, clarifying the *prātimokṣa* precepts for the five assemblies. Now, the first part.
If those sentient beings wish to practice the Mahāyāna path and seek to receive the fundamental bodhisattva heavy precepts,

as well as the vow to fully receive all prohibitory precepts for both lay and ordained persons— namely, the precept of restraining misconduct, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, and [the precept of benefiting sentient beings]— [they should do so].

Regarding the precept of gathering and transforming sentient beings: if one cannot find a virtuous and excellent preceptor who has extensively mastered the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas and previously practiced these teachings, one should, with a sincere mind within the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa), respectfully make offerings and look up to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, requesting them to act as preceptors and witnesses.
With single-minded resolve, one should establish the vow and recite the characteristics of the precepts, first declaring the ten root offenses.
The Heavy Precepts: Next, one should generally enumerate the three categories of precepts (*śīla-skandha*) and receive them through a personal vow; by doing so, one also attains the precepts.
*Mahāyāna*—here translated as "Great Vehicle"—refers to those who wish to practice the path of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, who must receive the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-vidha-śīla*).
These are precisely the ten heavy and forty-eight light precepts of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. These are the Bodhisattva precepts.

Both the two groups of lay followers and the five groups of renunciants may receive and uphold these precepts; therefore, they are called the "all-encompassing prohibitions for both laity and renunciants.
If there is a precept-bestowing master within a thousand *li*, one should logically receive them from that person.
However, if there is no one who has previously understood or practiced them, one may receive them by oneself. If one has previously committed a grave, superior offense, one must...
One may only vow to receive [the precepts] after seeking the signs of the pure wheel.

If one has no grave, predominant offenses in this life, one may then, within the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to serve as witnesses and teachers, and self-vow to obtain the precepts.

This is consistent with the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra* (or *Śīlaskandha*) Sūtras, which emphasize the arousal of the bodhicitta; it differs from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which requires that one see auspicious signs before being permitted to do so.

This is the section on characteristics. △ Second, clarifying the Prātimokṣa precepts for the five assemblies, which has two parts: first, clarifying those who obtain them; second, distinguishing those who do not. The first part has two sections: first, those of full age obtain the two assemblies of precepts; second, those of incomplete age first obtain the three minor assemblies of precepts. If one is less than twenty years of age, they may receive the Śrāmaṇera precepts from the Bhikṣu-saṃgha or the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha. It arises from the single reality realm of the mind and takes that single reality realm as its basis.
That is to say, because of relying upon the single reality realm, there is that ignorance which fails to understand the one dharma-realm;

through erroneous conceptualization and reflection, it manifests false objects, and by means of discrimination and attachment, it accumulates the causes and conditions of karma, thereby giving rise to the six sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By means of these...

Based on these six consciousnesses, within the midst of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, there arise perceptions of the disagreeable, the agreeable, and those that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable; from these, the eighteen kinds of feeling are produced.
Regarding the fact that all numbers arise from the number one: a single unit alone does not constitute a number.
One plus one makes two; two plus one makes three; three plus one makes four; four plus one makes five;
and so on, proceeding indefinitely, such that there is nothing that does not originate from one. Taking one as the basis: in relation to one, there is two. And...

Thus, proceeding in this manner without end, there is no case where each position is not still one.

They fail to realize that it is because my own mind stirs with a single thought of delusion that, without awareness, the five arise from the one.

It is not that there is actually a Heaven existing outside the mind. Furthermore, because my own mind’s single thought of deluded stillness and deluded movement combine, [the subsequent stages arise]. Thus, [it is not external].
Awakening thus constitutes the six sense-faculties; it is not that there are external fruits existing apart from the mind. Why is this so?
That which is "delusory movement" is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the faculty capable of discrimination—namely, erroneous recollection and thought.

That which is "delusory stillness" is the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) that is grasped and clung to—namely, the presently manifest delusory objects. Thought acts as the producer, while the objects [are the produced].

As for the capacity to accomplish: first, obtaining five results in six, which gives rise to water; this constitutes the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*). Second, obtaining five results in seven, which gives rise to fire;

The place of birth immediately becomes the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). It takes the five faculties and five objects as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which then constitutes the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).
Thus, the six faculties are established instantaneously; in reality, there is no sequence of before or after, but they are merely described in terms of number based on deluded conceptualization.

The six consciousnesses arise from the mutual encounter of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). One attains the manifestation of the six objective spheres (*viṣaya*), each of which may be contrary, favorable, or neither contrary nor favorable.
