The true substance of the mind: furthermore, each and every sentient being possesses the entire body of the mind, not merely a small portion of it.
This is because the substance of the mind is absolute and beyond dependence; it cannot be divided or severed, as it is without spatial direction and is inconceivable.

It is like the sunlight, which shines everywhere throughout every crevice; within each and every crevice, one perceives the entire body and great function of the sun, not merely a small portion of it.
Furthermore, the sunlight perceived in a single kṣaṇa is the very same sunlight that has existed from time immemorial until now.
Apart from this present sunlight before one, there is no past [sunlight] whatsoever.
Where could the sunlight of the future be stored separately? Now, even that which is merely a physical phenomenon (rūpa-dharma), such as sunlight, is thus inconceivable;
how much more so the wondrous and spiritual nature of the single mind? It is also like the first day of the year in the human world.
Then all the people under heaven would collectively increase by one year. Yet, it is only within that single year that each individual attains their full measure;
one cannot divide this single year into many parts so that the people of the world each receive a small portion.
Nor can it be said that because the people of the world each increase by one year, they thereby collectively form many years.
Now, even that which is merely a provisional method, such as the passage of time, is already inconceivable; how much more so the true substance of the single mind?

Therefore, regardless of whether one is deluded, confused, or inverted, down to the most minute insects and sentient beings, the substance of the present momentary thought has, from the very beginning, neither arisen nor ceased. This is because it is free from all conceptual discrimination. It is not... [as before].
Only after attaining Buddhahood will one realize non-arising and non-ceasing, and even transcend conceptual discrimination.
That which is fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing is, for example, like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky. These flowers are themselves empty;

therefore, while the cataracts are present, the flowers were fundamentally unarisen. Even when the cataracts are cleared away, the flowers are fundamentally unceasing, because there is no real flower that could exist.
It is because they have ceased. Within the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, sentient beings delusively perceive arising and ceasing;
yet arising is truly non-arising, and ceasing is truly non-ceasing. Regarding that which is fundamentally pure by its own nature, it is like smoke and mist rising in empty space.
The nature of empty space is originally free from defilement. Within this purity, sentient beings falsely perceive defilement;

yet the self-nature of defilement is eternally pure. That which has been unobstructed and unhindered from the very beginning is like the false appearance of square or round space within square or round vessels;
the essence of space is originally neither square nor round. Thus, within the unobstructed essence, sentient beings [perceive obstructions].
Delusory views constitute an obstruction; yet this obstruction is itself non-obstruction. This is because it is like space, free from conceptual discrimination.
For example, space transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; it cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist.
It has no boundaries; it is without movement; it has no form or substance; it has no directions or quarters; it has no "this" or "that"; it has no interior or exterior;
it is without birth or extinction; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither exists nor does not exist. It is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is beyond discrimination.
The present single thought-moment of the mind-nature of all sentient beings is also like this. This is the direct pointing.
The essence of the mind in this present moment of delusion and inverted confusion has been thus from the beginning. Therefore it is said:
"All sentient beings have realized perfect enlightenment. And again: "When a Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he sees all sentient beings as having attained perfect enlightenment.
Only in this way is there the direct pointing to the human mind and the seeing of nature to become Buddha. If one departs from the present...
To speak separately of the true mind apart from the preceding thought—how is this different from seeking water apart from the waves? △ Second, revealing the magnitude of the nature:
it is equal and universally pervasive, reaching everywhere; it fills the ten directions, is ultimately of one single mark, and is without duality or distinction.
It is neither changing nor different; it neither increases nor decreases.

This directly points to the essence of the present thought-moment of sentient beings, which has from the beginning vertically exhausted the past and horizontally pervaded all space, and cannot be confined or limited.
Although this present thought-moment, when sought, is utterly ungraspable, it universally knows all things.
The entire root-body and the vessel-world are left without exception. It is like the light of the eyes that clearly perceives the objects before it;
this light is perfectly complete, free from both aversion and attachment. Therefore it is said: "Equally and universally pervasive, reaching everywhere, it fills the ten directions.
Furthermore, when perceiving form, one knows it is not form; when perceiving sound, one knows it is not sound.
When one knows fragrance, one knows it is not fragrance; when one knows flavor, one knows it is not flavor; when one knows touch, one knows it is not touch;
when one knows mental objects (*dharma*), one knows they are not mental objects. Therefore, it is called the ultimate single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, among form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental objects, there is no knower, nor is there any non-knower; they cannot be divided.

It cannot be analyzed or pointed out; therefore, it is said that there is neither duality nor distinction. Furthermore, when one’s hair turns white and the face wrinkles, one knows that the essence has no wrinkles;
when the six sense-objects shift and perish, one knows that the essence has no shifting. Therefore, it is said that it does not shift and does not change.

Moreover, when it universally conditions the Dharma-realm, one knows that the essence does not expand; when the chamber of the pure mind is quieted, one knows that the essence does not contract. Therefore, it is said that there is no increase.
There is no decrease. △ Third, the manifestation of the inherent nature:

because the minds of all sentient beings, the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the minds of all bodhisattvas, and the minds of all buddhas are identical as the mark of true suchness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure.
This directly points to the essence of the single thought-moment before us, which inherently and spontaneously possesses the ten dharma-realms.

All sentient beings constitute the six realms of ordinary existence; together with śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—these ten realms are all identical to the true suchness (tathatā) of the present single thought-moment, which is neither arising nor ceasing, and neither defiled nor pure.
Apart from this present single thought-moment—the essence of the mind—no other ten dharma-realm minds can be found.
Therefore, if one refers to the Buddhas, the remaining nine realms are all the nine realms within the Buddha’s own mind;
there is nothing among these nine realms that is not possessed by the Buddha-mind. If one refers to those in hell, the remaining nine realms are likewise all the minds of hell.
Regarding the nine realms within the middle [of the ten realms]: there is not one of these nine realms that is not fully contained within the mind of a hell-being.
The same principle may be applied to know the remaining eight realms. It is like a single room containing ten lamps:

the light of any one lamp necessarily encompasses the lights of the other nine, such that they become a single light, mutually present and mutually fused. Furthermore, since one realm already contains all nine realms...

Thus, those nine realms, by their very nature (*dharmatā*), must also necessarily possess each other mutually; this constitutes the hundred realms. If one discusses the ten suchnesses for each realm, this constitutes the thousand suchnesses.

With respect to the five aggregates as substantial phenomena (*dravyadharma*), they also possess the thousand suchnesses. With respect to sentient beings as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), they also possess the thousand suchnesses.
With respect to the land of the supporting environment (*niśraya-bhājana-loka*), they also possess the thousand suchnesses; this is the "three thousand."
The nature and characteristics [of all phenomena] are, in their entirety, not separate from the substance of the present moment of mind.

It is like the sunlight within a single crack, which instantaneously encompasses the entire body of the sun; thus, it must necessarily encompass the entire bodies of the suns within hundreds of thousands of cracks, all returning to this one crack.
Furthermore, it must likewise encompass all that is pervaded by each of those suns within every individual crack.
The functional capacity to illuminate hundreds of thousands of apertures is entirely contained within this single aperture.

Furthermore, the all-pervading and omnipresent functional capacities existing in every single moment of the past and future must likewise be entirely contained within this one aperture and this one moment; they absolutely cannot be partitioned, for there is no division or limit.
The initial revelation of the Real is concluded. △ Second, the reconciliation of the delusory: Part One, reconciling the delusory as emptiness; Part Two, reconciling the delusory as the provisional;

Part Three, reconciling the delusory as the Middle. Emptiness means there is nothing that is not the measure of nature; the provisional means there is nothing that is not the endowment of nature; the Middle means there is nothing that is not the substance of nature.
Previously, when the Real was revealed, the Real encompassed the extremities of the delusory; now, when the delusory is reconciled, the delusory [is seen to be identical with the Real].

Because the true source thoroughly encompasses the deluded branches, the single reality is nothing other than the realm of experience; because the deluded reaches the true source, the realm of experience is nothing other than the single reality.
In the first section, delusion is immediately realized as empty. This has two parts: first, clarifying that awareness and cognition are empty;
second, clarifying that the realm of experience is empty—that is, the five aggregates are fundamentally empty. Now, the first part.
Why is this? All that arises from the mind as conceptualization is like a magical illusion; it possesses no reality.

This refers to the dharmas of consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, recollection, objective consideration, cognition, and so forth—these various mental factors are neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white, nor are they of variegated colors. They have no length or shortness, nor squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness, and so on.
If one were to exhaustively search throughout all worlds in the emptiness of the ten directions for the shape and form of the mind, not a single distinct portion could be found.
It is only due to the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming of sentient beings' ignorance and deluded darkness that false objects appear, causing them to give rise to attachment.
That is to say, this mind cannot know itself, yet it falsely claims to exist, giving rise to the notion of awareness and calculating "self."
Regarding "what belongs to me" (*ātmīya*): in reality, it possesses no characteristic of cognition or awareness, because this deluded mind ultimately lacks substance and cannot be perceived.

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign kings of the mind. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) and "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refer to two of the five omnipresent mental factors. "Formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the remaining [mental factors].

There are forty-nine mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). Although these minds and mental factors possess recollection, objective referents, and cognitive awareness, they are not manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*);
therefore, they are neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor variegated colors. Nor are they shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*);

therefore, they lack length, shortness, squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness. Furthermore, they do not exist in internal, external, or intermediate locations; therefore, they have no spatial configuration or boundaries.
If it were divisible, then there would be only the name "cognition," but in reality there would be no characteristic of cognition;
it would ultimately lack substance and could not be found even when sought. It is like waves, which have water as their substance and possess no separate self-substance of their own.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations" is intended precisely to reveal that this deluded mind has no substantial essence.

If one realizes its lack of essence, one will certainly not mistakenly take the reflected image resulting from one's own inference to be the inferring subject itself. △ Second, clarifying the emptiness of objective realms.
If there were no cognizing subject capable of discrimination, then there would be no differentiated characteristics of all objects throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
As previously stated,
the manifestation of delusory objects through the causes and conditions of perfuming occurs because all manner of phenomena arise from the mind.
Furthermore, it is said that this causes the arising of attachment through the production of thoughts; because these arise from dharmas, various kinds of minds are produced.

Yet, while the objective realm may still seem capable of being pointed out or described, the deluded mind ultimately cannot be found upon investigation. This is a case of negating the mind, not negating the realm.
Now it is clarified that it is due to discrimination that one falsely perceives the distinctions within the realm; since there is no actual cognition [of such distinctions], [the realm is not real].
As for that which is capable of discerning, how could there be an objective realm to be discerned? It is like the absence of sight—how could there be visible form?
It is like the absence of hearing—how could there be sound? Thus, both mind and objects are simultaneously negated, and the five aggregates are all empty.

It is not that things become empty only after they have been extinguished. This concludes the first section: "The Delusive is Immediately Empty. II. The Delusive is Immediately Provisional (again in three parts):

A. Because the mind is primary, objects are provisional; B. Because objects are primary, the mind is provisional; C. A triple re-demonstration of Mind-Only. Now, the first part: "Because the mind is primary, objects are provisional."
Because all phenomena cannot exist of themselves, but exist only through the discrimination of the deluded mind—
meaning that all objects do not each conceive of themselves as existing, yet know this as "self" and that as "other"—
all phenomena cannot exist of themselves and thus have no distinction; they depend solely upon the deluded mind, which fails to know and fail to understand the internal.

Because they do not exist inherently. This means that there are external objects of knowledge prior [to consciousness], yet one falsely gives rise to various conceptualizations of phenomena—conceiving of them as existent or non-existent, as "that" or "this," as "right" or "wrong," as good or evil, and so forth, until one falsely gives rise to immeasurable and boundless conceptualizations of phenomena.
One should understand all dharmas in this way: they all arise from false imagination and depend upon the deluded mind.
"Fundamentally,
not knowing and not comprehending that [the self] is internally non-existent" means falsely identifying the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body,
and falsely identifying the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind. Based on this internal non-existence, one falsely discriminates.

Apart from the external, there is no further "external. Yet, one gives rise to various mental states—existence and non-existence, this and that, right and wrong, good and evil—regarding these various phenomena.
Such dharmas do not truly arise; they arise only from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Since even deluded conceptualization cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be any dharma that arises? There are only provisional names and objective spheres. 2. Relying on the Objective Sphere.
Therefore, the mind is provisional.
Since this deluded mind lacks any intrinsic characteristic, it also exists in dependence upon objects;
that is to say, because it cognizes and perceives preceding objects through conditioned thought, it is designated as "mind."
This is what is meant by saying that the mind is fundamentally unborn, yet exists due to objects.
Although it is conventionally called "mind," when sought ultimately, it cannot be found at all, because it is neither color nor shape, and it exists neither internally, externally, nor in between.
There is only the provisional designation of "mind" and "mental factors. (△ This is the third section, further clarifying that there is only mind.)

Furthermore, although this deluded mind and the aforementioned objects mutually depend upon one another and arise without temporal sequence, this deluded mind is able to serve as the source and master of all objects.

Why is this so? It is because, based on the deluded mind’s failure to realize that the dharma-realm is of a single characteristic, it is said that the mind possesses ignorance (*avidyā*). Due to the causal power of ignorance, deluded objects manifest; and likewise, they depend upon—

Because ignorance ceases, all objective spheres cease. It is not because one does not understand objective spheres for oneself that it is said that ignorance exists with respect to objective spheres; nor does ignorance arise dependent upon objective spheres. This is because all Buddhas...
Because ignorance does not arise with respect to any object, and because it does not depend on the cessation of objects, the mind of ignorance ceases;
for all objects have been self-extinguished by their very nature from the beginning, never having existed at all.
Based on this principle, it is therefore said that all phenomena take the mind as their fundamental basis.
The previous explanation clarified that objects exist based on the deluded mind; thus, the mind arises and phenomena arise, which can be termed "Mind-Only.
The subsequent explanation clarifies that the deluded mind exists based on objects; thus, phenomena arise and the mind arises, which seems not to accord with the meaning of "Mind-Only."

Therefore, although they both mutually depend upon one another, it is now clarified that the mind remains the primary factor. One should know that the objective realm exists in dependence upon the deluded mind;

thus, the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) acts as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the transformation into the objective division (*nimittabhāga*). The deluded mind exists in dependence upon the objective realm;

thus, the objective division acts as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the manifestation of the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*). In this way, the two divisions—the seen and the seeing—arise.

They must be simultaneous; therefore, there is no priority or posteriority. This deluded mind subsumes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the two internal parts [the self-verifying part and the self-evidencing part], and is collectively termed "mind.
It is only by referring to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) that it is designated as the "object.

Since both the seeing and the image arise based upon the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti*), there is no object distinct from the mind. Thus, it is said that all phenomena depend entirely upon the mind. Question: Since...
If it is said that there is "only mind," why does the Tiantai school further speak of "only form" and "only fragrance"? Answer:

It is precisely because the objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the six sense-objects arise in dependence upon the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and their essence is itself mind; therefore, "only form" and "only fragrance" are still "only mind.
Thus, there is no contradiction. If one were to reckon that form and fragrance possess separate intrinsic natures, how could one then cause all [phenomena]...?
The Dharma-trend. Now, based on the single mind, there exist appearances and views; these various appearances and views are entirely the mind itself.
Therefore, they can mutually contain, mutually enter, mutually pervade, and mutually merge. This concludes the second section: "Subsuming Delusion as the Provisional.

△ Third, subsuming delusion as the Middle. This has two parts: first, subsuming through the realization of the meaning; second, subsuming through the realization of dependent origination. Herein is the first.
One should know that all phenomena are entirely termed "mind," because their meaning and essence are not different, as they are all subsumed within the mind.

That their meaning is not different means that they are equally phenomena produced by causes and conditions, and equally—each and every one—are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.
"Substance is not different" means that they share the same substance, which is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

"Being subsumed by the mind" means that both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise based on the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*); by subsuming the branches and returning to the root, they are collectively termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Consciousness-only is precisely mind-only (*cittamātra*). 2. Second, the reconciliation from the perspective of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind and manifest as its characteristics; they exist through conjunction, arising and ceasing together, and likewise lack any abiding.
This is because all objective realms merely follow what the mind takes as its object, continuing in succession from moment to moment.
Thus it abides and is maintained; it exists for a moment.
Arising from the mind, it arises from the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) as the objective image-division (*nimittabhāga*).

It acts as an image for the mind, serving as the immediate objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*). They exist in conjunction, meaning that the mind cannot be differentiated [from them].
The "boundary" refers to the limits of the objective field (*viṣaya*). "Arising together and ceasing together" means that within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), there is no sequence of before and after.
"Equally lacking abiding" means that the mind and its objects do not fail to perish as soon as they first arise; they never migrate into a second moment.
The mind and objects of the second moment merely continue in a succession similar to the preceding moment; for this reason, they appear to be permanent and appear to be a unity.

Those who are ignorant do not know this; they falsely reckon it to be permanent and unitary. This concludes the first section: Clarifying the Substance. II. Clarifying the Characteristics (Phenomena).
A. First, stating the names. B. Second, detailed explanation. C. Third, reconciling the explanations. Now, the first [section].
Regarding the meaning of "mind" as thus explained, there are two kinds of characteristics. What are these two? First, the internal characteristic of mind;
second, the external characteristic of mind. As for the internal characteristic of mind, it further has two kinds. What are these two? First, the true [nature].

The second is delusion. The preceding section clarified the essence of the sentient beings' mind: its essence is without discrimination; its measure encompasses all horizontal and vertical dimensions; it fully possesses the ten realms;

and when delusion is entirely present, it is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—beyond conceptualization. How, then, can one discuss its characteristics? Yet, because it is without characteristics, there is nothing [to grasp].
They are not distinct; therefore, two kinds of characteristics can exist. One should know that these two characteristics are both, in fact, without characteristics.
For this reason, it is called the "Greatness of Characteristics. As for the internal characteristic of the mind, it does not actually exist within;

however, because the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) and the portion verifying the self-verification (*svasaṃvittisvasaṃvittibhāga*) are subtle, profound, and secret, they cannot be seen. Therefore, it is called the internal characteristic of the mind. [The external characteristic of the mind...]

As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), they do not actually exist externally; however, because the functions of the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are manifest and are universally acknowledged by the world, they are called "external characteristics of the mind.
Since both internal and external characteristics are equally termed "mind," there is nothing else whatsoever outside the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the true and the false within the internal object-aspect: the "true" refers to all minds and...
The ontological substance that serves as the basis for the fourfold enumeration is also called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Although this reality pervades both internal and external aspects, it is provisionally termed "internal" because it is subtle and secret. Delusion consists of the various minds and mental factors, each having two internal parts;

these arise from being deluded regarding the truth and take true suchness (*tathatā*) as their substance. Since they have no separate self-substance of their own, they are called "delusory. This delusion...
Furthermore, it has no spatial dimensions or boundaries; because it cannot be seen, it is provisionally termed "internal. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the three [aspects]:
first, the explanation of the True; second, the explanation of the False; third, the explanation of external appearances. Now, the first.

That which is called "the Real" refers to the fundamental nature of the mind's essence. It is suchness (*tathatā*), unchanging, pure and perfect, unobstructed and unhindered, subtle and secret, difficult to perceive.
Because it pervades all places, is eternal and indestructible, and establishes and gives rise to all phenomena, it is so named.
In clarifying the essence (*tattva*) above, all arising and ceasing are subsumed and returned to True Suchness (*tathatā*), because there is no arising and ceasing outside of True Suchness.
Now, in clarifying the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), all True Suchness is subsumed and returned to arising and ceasing, because there is no True Suchness outside of arising and ceasing.
That which is called "True" is equivalent to the meaning of "Awakening" as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*.

The fundamental characteristic of the essence of mind is precisely what is called the state free from conceptual thought (*niṣprapañca*). It is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
Since it is the single characteristic of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is said to be "suchness" (*tathatā*), non-differentiated, pure, perfect, and so forth.
This very meaning of awakening (*bodhi*) is able to encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena; therefore, it is said that it "establishes and brings forth" them all.
It is the essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, that which is not different from suchness is the substance of the nature; its perfection and difficulty of perception is the magnitude of the nature;
its establishment and growth is the inherent possession of the nature. △ Second, the explanation of delusion.
What is called "falsehood" refers to the arising of conceptualization, discrimination, cognition, objective consideration, recollection, and imagination.
Although these continue in succession and can give rise to all manner of various objects, they are internally hollow and deceptive, lacking any reality because they cannot be perceived.

What is called "delusion" (mṛṣā) is equivalent to the meaning of "non-awakening" (abodhi) as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*. The arising of thought is precisely the "phase of karma" (karmalakṣaṇa).
When the non-awakened mind moves, it is designated as "karma"; this refers to each of the primary minds and mental factors (citta-caitta), which each possesses two internal divisions.

Discernment, cognition, objective consideration, and recollective conceptualization constitute the "phase of the seer" (darśanalakṣaṇa); these are present within each of the primary minds and mental factors.
The "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is this [subjective aspect]. All objective realms that arise from it are the "object-aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*);

this refers to the fact that each mind and mental factor possesses its own object-aspect. As for the statement that "the internal is false and lacks reality," it means that non-enlightenment exists by virtue of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
Thought lacks intrinsic characteristics and does not depart from fundamental enlightenment; if one were to depart from the nature of enlightenment, there would be no non-enlightenment.
Therefore, this non-awakening has no separate, real self-substance that can be perceived. △ Third, the explanation of external appearances:
What are called "external appearances apart from the mind" refers to all dharmas, various objects of experience, and so forth, which arise according to whatever is being thought of.
Because objects appear before one, we know that there is an internal mind and its various distinctions.

Whatever is contemplated, the object appears before one; this is precisely the arising of the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) based upon the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying aspect). Thus, we know that there is an internal mind and its various distinctions.
It is by means of the *nimittabhāga* as the object of cognition (*ālambana*) that the existence of the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*) is revealed.

The *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is like the light of a mirror; the *nimitta-bhāga* (objectified aspect) is like the reflection in the mirror. Therefore, it is called the "external appearance" of the mind, not because it exists outside the mind.
The *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect) is like the surface of the mirror, and the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga* (aspect that verifies the self-verifying aspect) is like the back of the mirror.
Therefore, it is called the internal characteristic of the mind; it does not mean that it exists within the mind.

For example, the front and back of a mirror have copper as their substance and possess no separate intrinsic nature of their own; thus, they are called "delusive. Fundamental Awakening (mūla-avabodha) and True Suchness (tathatā) are like the copper of the mirror.
Therefore, it is called "true. When the false is subsumed within the true, whether it be the back or the front, the luster or the image, there is nothing that is not copper.
Thus, the gate of arising and ceasing is the gate of suchness (*tathatā*). When the false arises based on the true, it is simply this one piece of copper.
Whether it be the back, the front, the light, or the image, the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha) is itself the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha-mukha).

When distinguished according to their characteristics (lakṣaṇa), the copper, the back, and the front all belong to the essence (svabhāva); therefore, they are called "internal characteristics. The light and the image both belong to the function (vṛtti);
therefore, they are called "external characteristics. The second section, the detailed explanation, is concluded. △ Third, the reconciliation of the two [gates]. First, the direct [explanation]...
Regarding the two aspects of the external meeting and returning to the internal, we now address the first:
the meeting with external appearances. One should know this: internal delusory appearances act as the cause and the essence, while external delusory appearances act as the effect and the function.
Based on these meanings, I therefore say that all dharmas are collectively termed "mind.

Cause and effect, essence and function, are all subsumed within the single mind; there is no dharma outside the mind. This reveals that this mind has no external characteristics, which is called the "Greatness of Characteristics" (xiàng-dà).
△ Second, reconciling with principle through external characteristics, which is further divided into three parts. First, reconciling the essential nature (xìng-tǐ):
Second, the nature and magnitude; third, the nature and endowment. Regarding the first:
furthermore, one should know that external phenomena apart from the mind are like the various objects seen in a dream—they are produced solely by the mind’s conceptualization.

There are no external objects that possess substantial reality. All objective spheres are likewise thus, for they are all produced by the deluded imaginings of consciousness—which, like a dream, arises based upon ignorance.

Furthermore, one should know that because the internal mind does not abide for even a single moment, all perceived and conditioned objects also do not abide for a single moment following the mind. That is to say: "When the mind arises, various phenomena arise."
Because the mind ceases, the various phenomena cease; this is the characteristic of arising and ceasing. It exists only as a name, for in reality it cannot be apprehended.
Since the mind does not go out to reach objects, and objects do not come in to reach the mind, they are like reflections in a mirror—neither coming nor going.
Therefore, if one seeks the fixed characteristics of arising and ceasing within all phenomena, they are utterly unfindable. This is what is called "one."
All phenomena are ultimately without substance; they are originally and eternally empty, for they truly neither arise nor perish.

Consequently, all sentient beings are perpetually deluded by external appearances and fail to realize that these are but mind-only. Therefore, it is necessary to further bring them back to the single principle.
The passage beginning with "Like what is seen in a dream" establishes the analogy; the passage beginning with "All objective realms" applies this to the dharma. Furthermore...
Next, it should be understood that what follows below further clarifies that the objective realm is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing.
Because the mind arises, the various phenomena arise; thus, it is only the mind that arises, and there are no separate phenomena that arise.
Because the mind ceases, the various phenomena cease; thus, it is only the mind that ceases, and there are no separate phenomena that can cease. Therefore, it is said: "All phenomena arise from..."
Originally, it is eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction. It is further said: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
Like an image in a mirror, its substance is nothing but bronze; how could there ever have been arising? How could there ever have been ceasing?
△ Second, reconciling the nature and the measure.
If all phenomena are thus truly without arising or ceasing, then there would be no characteristics of differentiation among any objects;
they would be quiescent and of a single flavor, which is called *tathatā*, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*).
That intrinsically pure mind is profoundly still and perfect, because it is devoid of the characteristics of conceptual discrimination.
Suppose there is a single form seen by the eye or a single fragrance smelled by the nose. This form and this fragrance are, in reality, neither arising nor ceasing.
Since they neither arise nor cease, they are without differentiation; they are quiescent and of a single flavor.
They are thus *tathatā*, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and are inherently tranquil and perfect. Therefore it is said: "In every form and every fragrance, there is [no duality]."
This is not the Middle Way. The essence of the Middle Way has no divisions or limits; it expands like the great void and is therefore called the "measure of nature" (*xingliang*).
As it is with color and fragrance, so it is with every phenomenon (*dharmas*). △ Third, harmonizing the inherent possession of nature.

That which is without the mark of conceptual differentiation is omnipresent in all places. Its omnipresence consists in its ability to serve as the support and foundation for the establishment of all phenomena.

If even a single color or a single fragrance expands to be identical with empty space and is devoid of discriminative characteristics, then it must be omnipresent and universally capable of serving as the support and foundation for the establishment of all dharmas. Therefore, it is said: "All dharmas tend toward form;
this tendency is unsurpassed. "All dharmas tend toward fragrance; this tendency is unsurpassed. Because they serve as the support and foundation, they are so named.

Regarding the inherent nature (*prakṛti-yukta*): as it is with form and fragrance, so it is with every phenomenon (*dharma*). Now, since all phenomena are in reality neither arising nor ceasing, causes and conditions are themselves the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
Since all phenomena lack the characteristic of discrimination, causes and conditions are themselves emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Since all phenomena are able to serve as the support and foundation for the establishment of all other phenomena, causes and conditions are themselves the provisional (*prajñapti*). If even the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is thus, how much more so the subjective aspect!
How much more so for the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)? How much more so for the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the verifying-of-self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*)?

It is clear that the characteristics of these four parts of all minds and mental factors are identical to the single, true characteristic of the objective realm. This concludes the second section, the clarification of the characteristics. △ Third, the clarification of the treasury (*garbha*). 1.

This is because the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas, from the beginningless primordial limit, has been without...
Unobstructed by hindrances, sovereign and indestructible, all manifestations and various meritorious deeds are perpetually blazing and never cease.
This is because they universally display activities throughout all worlds for the sake of various transformative benefits.
Thus, the body of one Buddha is the body of all Buddhas, and the bodies of all Buddhas are the body of one Buddha.
All activities performed are likewise identical, namely, characterized by non-discrimination. They do not involve thoughts of self or other;
they are equal and non-dual. Because they arise based on the single *dharmatā*, these activities are identical to spontaneous transformation (*nirmita*), for their essence is without distinction.
That mind refers precisely to the single thought-moment of the present in sentient beings.
The substance of this single thought-moment of sentient beings is fully endowed with the karma of untainted merit; it is the Tathāgatagarbha, which is equal and non-dual.
The Buddhas realize this and take it as their Dharmakāya; it is nothing other than the full realization of the fundamental nature of all sentient beings.
This principle has existed from time immemorial: its characteristic is fundamentally unobstructed and unhindered; its essence is fundamentally sovereign and indestructible;
and its function is fundamentally manifested in all transformations. It does not come into being only after one attains Buddhahood. However, although all sentient beings equally rely upon it...
This dharma-nature, due to false discrimination and the deluded thought of "this" and "that," is erroneously reckoned as distinct within its single essence.
The Buddhas have already shattered the two attachments to self and phenomena, severed the source of ignorance, and realized this single nature;

"In this way, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas pervades all places because it is perfectly complete and immovable; therefore, it follows the deaths of all sentient beings..."
This gives rise to that, constantly serving as its support.

It is only because sentient beings dwell in delusion and lack awakening that, with respect to...
That which all Buddhas realize manifests as the Dharmakāya. This very Dharmakāya, when it transmigrates through the six realms, is called a sentient being.
If there were no Dharmakāya of the Buddhas to serve as its basis, how could there be the death here and birth there of sentient beings? 2. Establishing a Simile.
It is like space, which can fully contain all forms and images of every variety of shape and kind;

for all forms and images of every variety of shape and kind depend upon space for their establishment and growth, abide within space, are encompassed by the realm of space, and have space as their very substance.
There is nothing that can transcend the boundaries of the realm of space. Thus it should be understood.
One knows that within the realm of forms and appearances, the sphere of empty space cannot be destroyed. When forms and appearances perish, they return to empty space;
yet the fundamental sphere of empty space neither increases nor decreases, remaining unmoving and unchanging.

Here, empty space is borrowed as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas; and their material forms and physical types are borrowed as metaphors for the karmic retribution and afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings. △ Third, the application of the analogy.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is likewise: it is able to contain and receive the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings.

Because the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings are established and grow in dependence upon the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, they abide within the Dharma-body and are encompassed by the sphere of the Dharma-body. Taking the Dharma-body as their essence, there is nothing that can transcend it.
Regarding the constituent element of the Dharma-body: one should know that within the bodies of all sentient beings, the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is likewise indestructible.
When afflictions are severed and eliminated, they return to the Dharma-body; yet the fundamental realm of the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases, remaining unmoving and unchanging.

This uses the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas to correspond to the analogy of empty space; it uses the karmic retribution of sentient beings to correspond to the analogy of their physical forms and appearances.
Because they are established and grow in dependence upon the *dharmakāya*, they are called "identical to the provisional" (*jia*).

Because they are subsumed within the locus of the *dharmakāya*, they are called "identical to emptiness" (*kong*). Because the *dharmakāya* is their essence, they are called "identical to the Middle" (*zhong*). [This applies to] the bodies of sentient beings.
The central dharmakāya cannot be destroyed; therefore, it is originally without decrease. When afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, one returns to the dharmakāya;
therefore, there is also no increase. Due to afflictions, one falsely perceives various karmic retributions within the dharmakāya.
Although these retributions appear to move, the dharmakāya does not move; although these retributions appear to change, the dharmakāya does not [change].
Transformation. It is like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky; the appearance of the flowers flutters and seems to move, yet the sky is fundamentally unmoving.
The appearance of the flowers arises and perishes and seems to change, yet the sky is fundamentally unchanging. Question:

Question: Regarding the *dharmakāya*, why do you say it is the severance and destruction of afflictions (*kleśa*)? Answer: The retribution-body has no substantial nature; its very substance is entirely the *dharmakāya*.
Because of afflictions, one does not see that the substance of the retribution-body is the *dharmakāya*.
When afflictions are severed and completely exhausted, one then perceives that every pore of the body is equal in measure to empty space, universally containing all lands and atoms. It is not...
This is inconceivable. How could there be any further retribution that could be destroyed, such that it would expand to become identical to inert emptiness?
Question: Even if one were to say that when retribution is destroyed, it returns to the *dharmakāya*, what fault would there be in that? Answer: There is a fault.

If the afflictions (*kleśa*) have not been severed, then at the time the retribution is destroyed, another maturation (*vipāka*) will arise again. How, then, could one realize and unite with the *dharmakāya*?
If afflictions are severed, then this illusory, empty body is fundamentally the Dharma-body; what need is there to wait for the further destruction of karmic retribution? Question:
In this case, there is the fault that the dharma and the metaphor are not equivalent. Answer: Generally speaking, a metaphor is merely a partial similarity.
For example, when a snow mountain is used as a metaphor for an elephant, how can one demand that it possess a tail or tusks? Or when the full moon is used as a metaphor for a face?
How could one seek its eyebrows and eyes? Now, the Dharma-body is compared to empty space; how could one demand that it possess conscious intelligence or quiescent illumination?

One should know that the substance of the present single thought-moment of sentient beings is precisely the ultimate Dharma-body realized by all Buddhas—absolute, true, and eternal, beyond all analogy. It is only because it is self-concealed by afflictions that [it appears otherwise].

Yet they do not understand this; therefore, having no other choice, I must employ various metaphors. To clarify that the entire substance follows conditions, I use the analogy of gold being cast into images of the ten realms.
However, I still fear that those who are deluded might think there is actual fabrication or that there are distinct boundaries.
To clarify that [the response] appears immediately upon encountering [the stimulus], it is illustrated by the analogy of a mirror reflecting beautiful or ugly features.

Yet, fearing that the deluded might still think there is a distinction between self and other, or between internal and external, one clarifies that delusion and awakening have no inherent nature by using the analogies of empty flowers arising and ceasing, or ice and water transforming into one another.
Still, fearing that the deluded might think that delusion can produce awakening, or that awakening can likewise produce delusion, [the text proceeds].
If one desires clear wisdom that is indestructible, it is likened to gold extracted from ore or wood reduced to ash;
yet, fearing that those who are deluded might claim that one part is permanent while another part is impermanent, no verbal designation whatsoever can reach this truth.
It is like a blind man attempting to discern the color of milk: hearing of a crane, he says it is moving; hearing of snow, he says it is cold. Hearing...
Seeing flour, one thinks it is soft; hearing a conch shell, one thinks it is hard. Through such various conceptualizations, one can never perceive the true color of the milk.

This refers to the fact that if one attempts to discern perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*) without having realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that nature of perfect enlightenment will itself become subject to cyclic flow. Now, as there is no other way, I shall provide further assistance.
This single commentary on "Contemplating the Mind" enables those of wisdom to directly realize it:
the substance of the present single thought-moment is fully capable of containing the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings.
This is because the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings are all established and grow in dependence upon the substance of the present single thought-moment, abiding within the present.
Within the substance of the single thought-moment, it is subsumed by the substance of this present single thought-moment;

This essence of the present single thought-moment is the fundamental realm (*dhātu*); it neither increases nor decreases, and is immovable and unchanging. Think on this, think on this! Question:

If the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*) is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and does not require extinction, then afflictions are themselves *prajñā*. Why, then, must they be severed? Answer:
If one knows that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves *prajñā*, then when *prajñā* manifests, there are no longer any afflictions; this is called the cessation of afflictions.
This is merely a discussion of "cessation" in the sense of being neither extinguished nor non-extinguished. How could there truly be a substantial entity of affliction that could be extinguished?
Again, he asked: "If afflictions are neither extinguished nor non-extinguished, yet one can still speak of their cessation, then..."
The retribution is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished. Why, then, is its extinction not discussed? Answer: Afflictions are like forms; retribution is like shadows.
Afflictions are like sounds; retribution is like echoes. Afflictions are like cataracts in the eye; retribution is like flowers in the sky.
Therefore, one discusses only the extinction of afflictions; there is no need to further discuss the extinction of retribution. Question: By means of empty space...

second, it is neither born nor extinguished; third, there is nowhere it does not pervade; fourth, it encompasses all without exterior; fifth, it is unobstructed and unimpeded; sixth, it cannot be grasped or touched. These are the points of similarity.

The Dharma-body universally encompasses four parts of the mind and mental factors, for these four parts are none other than the substance of the Dharma-body;

this is precisely what is meant by "not being similar. If one can thoroughly realize that these four parts are none other than the Dharma-body, then even this objective part (nimitta-bhāga) of empty space is the entire body of the Dharma-body, not merely a small portion of it. Emptiness is identical to the great void of the ten directions; it is identical to the myriad forms of the ten realms.

How could this be the emptiness that is conceptually reckoned as a counterpart to form by the deluded sentiments of afflictions? Second, the explanation of the possession [of the nine] within the Buddha-realm is concluded.

△ Third, the explanation of the ten realms from the perspective of delusion and enlightenment has two parts: first, explaining the distinctions between delusion and enlightenment; second, explaining ultimate equality.
The first section also has two parts: first, six ordinary beings categorized by the perfuming of ignorance; second, four noble ones categorized by the perfuming of the Dharma-body.
Now, for the first part:
from time immemorial, it has coexisted with the mind of ignorance; due to the power of the perfuming of the causes and conditions of deluded darkness, it manifests.

Regarding false objects: because they rely on the causal conditions of the habitual perfuming of false objects, a mind associated with delusion arises, which conceives of "self" and "what belongs to self," accumulates various karmas, and undergoes the suffering of birth and death. That Dharma-body is thus called a "sentient being."

Regarding the mind of ignorance (*avidyā-citta*): because of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), there arises non-awakening, which is the fundamental dwelling-place ignorance (*mūla-vāsabhūmi-avidyā*).
This is what is called the "affliction of identical substance" (*tongti-huo*) existing outside the realms (*dhātu*).

Due to this fundamental ignorance, which is the mental state of delusion, the entire body of the *dharma-kāya* becomes the aspect of karmic activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), thereby forming the self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*).

This refers to the internal essence of the *svasaṃvittivijñāna* (self-witnessing division). Due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) caused by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), the manifestation of false objects is precisely the perfuming of the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) by ignorance, which causes the essence of the mind and its mental factors to illusorily form the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
From the causal conditions of the habitual perfuming of these false objects, up to the conceptualization of "I" and "mine," [it arises] from...

From fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), there arises derivative ignorance (*śākhā-pratyaṅga-avidyā*), namely the clinging to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya-grāha*).

This refers to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realms. Regarding the accumulation of various karmas: through the condition of ignorance, there is volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*), whereby one creates the three types of out-flowing karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable (*sāsrava-kuśala-akuśala-āneñjya-karma*).

Regarding the experience of the suffering of birth and death: this refers to the segmented birth and death (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) within the three realms. [The text concludes with the character for] "joy" (*ruci*).

This is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Suffering itself is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). That which is neither pleasant nor painful is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
This is precisely the *dharmakāya* circulating through the six realms; therefore, it is called "sentient beings. If there were no *dharmakāya*, the very name "sentient beings" could not exist.
△ Second, regarding the perfuming of the *dharmakāya*, there are four types of sages.

If, among such sentient beings, those whose dharma-body熏習 (perfuming/imprregnation) is powerful, their afflictions gradually thin out; they are able to grow weary of the world and seek the path to nirvana;
they take refuge with faith in the single reality and cultivate the six pāramitās and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).
These are called bodhisattvas. Among such bodhisattvas, those who have fulfilled the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas [are further distinguished].
Those who have ultimately attained liberation from the sleep of ignorance are designated as Buddhas.
Regarding the perfuming of the Dharma-body: the Dharma-body is precisely the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).

Since there are no sentient beings who do not possess this nature of original enlightenment, they are able to receive the perfuming of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) processes of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Through such perfuming...

The power of cultivation (*abhyāsa-bala*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). It relies upon the fundamental enlightened nature (*prakṛti-bodhicitta*) to give rise to untainted supramundane wisdom (*anāsrava-lokottara-jñāna*), which no longer nourishes or perfumes the seeds of affliction (*kleśa-bīja*).
Consequently, afflictions gradually diminish. Because afflictions are diminished, one is able to cultivate weary detachment from the false and illusory fruits of the mundane world.
Although this weary detachment is the same [as that of others], there is a difference in the generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*). If it were otherwise...
If, from the beginning, one's attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is heavy, one first seeks the path to *nirvāṇa*.
If, from the beginningless past, one's attachment to phenomena is light, one is able to have faith in and take refuge in the single reality (*ekasatya*).

Regarding the distinctions in the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), those who seek *nirvāṇa* are called followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*), while those who believe in the single reality are called Bodhisattvas. Regarding their ultimate practice, however, they are one.
Gradual enlightenment and sudden enlightenment are both termed "Bodhisattvas. Upon ultimately departing from the sleep of ignorance, they change their name to "Buddha.
Even if there were no sentient beings, neither Bodhisattvas nor Buddhas could be found. This concludes the first section clarifying the distinction between delusion and enlightenment.
△ Second, clarifying ultimate equality.
One should know that such distinctions as between sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and buddhas exist only by virtue of worldly conventional designations and names;
yet the essence of the dharmakāya is ultimately equal, without any marks of difference.
The Dharma-body is likened to the nature of moisture; sentient beings are like ice; and the Buddha is like pure water.

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as Bodhisattvas, are like ice that is gradually melting but not yet exhausted. The moisture-nature of the ice does not diminish, and the moisture-nature of the water does not increase.
Therefore, it is said that they are ultimately equal. This may be called merely a transformation of names, devoid of any real nature. Part Two:
The Detailed Explanation is concluded. △ Three: The Summary.
"Good son, this is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the single reality realm."

By combining the preceding three meanings—the essence of mind, the characteristics of mind, and the *tathāgatagarbha*—one can briefly manifest the realm of the single reality (*ekasatya*) as the initial expedient for progress.
This concludes the first section: "Showing the Realm of Single Reality to Open the Perfect Understanding.
△ Second, showing the two kinds of contemplative paths to manifest the perfect practice. Part One: The direct explanation of the two contemplations.

This consists of three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the analytical discussion. Regarding the first: It is the perfectly round and correct practice that serves as the condition for obstructing the two crookednesses. This consists of three sections: first, the perfectly round skillful means; second, the auxiliary practices;
and third, the initial, middle, and final stages. First, the general heading.
If one wishes to cultivate faith and understanding based on the single reality of the objective realm, one should study two kinds of contemplative paths.
What are these two? First, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness; second, the contemplation of the true nature of suchness.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [contemplations]. First, the explanation of the contemplation of mind-only consciousness; second, the explanation of the contemplation of the reality of *tathatā*.

Regarding the first, there are three parts: first, the correct presentation of the contemplative gate; second, the superior progress upon the completion of the contemplation; third, the summary of the contemplative efficacy. Regarding the first [of these three], there are again three parts:

first, the observation that the object is mind-only; second, the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the mind; third, the accomplishment of the contemplative gate. Regarding the first [of these three], there are again three parts: first...
First, showing the object of observation; second, showing the observing contemplation; third, exhorting practice and avoiding faults. Regarding the first:
one who studies the contemplation of mind-only consciousness should, at all times and in all places, whatever actions they perform with body, speech, or mind, [observe them as such].
"At all times" refers to moments such as walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. "In all places" refers to locations such as seeing forms or hearing sounds.

Whatever actions are performed by means of body, speech, or mind—namely, the acts of fabrication, verbal expression, and mental apprehension—to put it briefly, they do not go beyond the six modes of activity and the six objects;
each and every one is nothing other than an object of contemplation. These are the six modes of activity.
These are: first, walking; second, standing; third, sitting; fourth, lying down; fifth, speaking; sixth, performing activities.
As for the six objects: first, seeing forms; second, hearing sounds; third, smelling odors; fourth, tasting flavors; fifth, feeling tangibles; sixth, cognizing dharmas.
Within these twelve matters, one must practice and study the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). △ Second, showing the contemplating subject and the contemplation.
One should thoroughly investigate and know that everything is but mind. Even regarding all objective spheres, if the mind dwells upon them, one should examine and know them all;
do not allow the mind to wander aimlessly toward indeterminate objects without self-awareness. In every moment of thought, one should observe accordingly:
whatever object the mind takes as its focus, one should cause the mind to follow that very thought, so that the mind knows itself.
Know that these mental conceptions arise spontaneously within one's own mind; it is not the case that all objective realms possess thought or discrimination.

What is meant is that within the internal mind, there spontaneously arise views of long and short, good and bad, right and wrong, gain and loss, decline and profit, existence and non-existence, and so forth—an infinity of such conceptions.
Yet, within all objective realms, there has never been a conception that gives rise to discrimination. One should know this for certain regarding all things.
Because the objective realm itself is devoid of discriminative thought, it is neither long nor short, neither beautiful nor ugly, and so forth, up to being neither existent nor non-existent;
it is free from all marks. Observing in this way, one sees that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions.
Were they to be separated from the mind, not a single phenomenon or mark could be seen to possess any differentiation of its own.

This "Contemplation of Mind-Only Consciousness" is the sharp blade that shatters attachment to phenomena, the fierce flame that incinerates afflictions, the essential ford for realizing *nirvāṇa*, and the secret key to attaining *bodhi*. It is most simple and easy; it is most wondrous and profound.
There are five sub-sections. The first states: "One should thoroughly observe and know that all is but mind," which generally demonstrates mind-only.

This is the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Next, it says, "up to the point where one does not even self-awaken to anything," which demonstrates the gate of insight into the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
If the mind dwells upon any object with mindfulness, it becomes the grasping of the imagined nature, which is termed "conceptualization.
Now, one must immediately examine and know [this], so as not to allow indeterminate攀緣 (clinging to objects) to remain unawakened; therefore, this is called "insight" (*vipaśyanā*).

This term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is not the same as the indeterminate nature among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Within the three natures, that which is indeterminate is so called because it cannot be designated as either wholesome or unwholesome;

thus, it is named "indeterminate. Here, however, by means of the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*), one maintains mindfulness within the internal mind, and this is termed "determination.
If, moreover, one forgets the contemplation of mind-only consciousness and falls into the proliferation of false conceptualizations and objective attachments, [it is no longer so].

Since beginningless time, sentient beings have failed to understand that the objects appearing before them are manifestations of their own minds;

thus, they can only give rise to false discrimination directed outwardly and are unable to turn back and contemplate the internal characteristics of their own minds. Now, through skillful cultivation...
The contemplation of mind-only consciousness means knowing that objects are but mind, so that the mind does not wander outward.
Thus, as soon as a thought arises, one recognizes it and does not drift away or fall under its sway. When the three root poisons—greed, hatred, and false views—arise, one recognizes them immediately;
upon recognition, one does not allow them to continue. This is why the *Āgama* sūtras value the recognition of evil, which is consistent with the wholesome qualities of faith, shame, and so forth.

That which is associated with dharmas [conducive to liberation] is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*). That which is associated with unwholesome dharmas such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) is called "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).

The preceding discussion on the cultivation of contemplation applied to all times and all places; now, however, with respect to entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), among the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), sitting is the most excellent.

By knowing that it is only the mind that arises, one realizes that form (*rūpa*) is fundamentally without arising; by knowing that it is only the mind that ceases, one realizes that form is fundamentally without cessation.

The flow of water and the flicker of a lamp do not abide for even a moment; they arise only for an instant and perish immediately thereafter, such that there is no possibility for them to move from this place to another.
Since there is no movement or transition, the characteristics of the mind are fundamentally quiescent. If the mind is fundamentally quiescent, how could form be otherwise?

By contemplating that form is nothing but mind, one awakens to its fundamental quiescence; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Quiescence of Form and Mind (*rūpa-citta-śānti-samādhi*). It does not mean—

Vipaśyanā is precisely the threefold contemplation within a single mind. Both are called "contemplating the mind" because both involve the illumination and clear realization of wisdom.
Both are referred to as "faith" because they point to the non-dual, wondrous śamatha and vipaśyanā within the stage of the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching.

Therefore, one should train in the two aspects of the mind of faith and contemplation, so that in every thought-moment one merges with the principle and in every thought-moment gives rise to its function, making them equal and upright, and swiftly ascending [to enlightenment].

Now, for the first:
regarding one who practices the contemplation of the mind through faith in *śamatha*, they contemplate that the internal mind has no visible characteristics; it is perfectly complete and immovable.
There is no coming and no going; its fundamental nature is neither arising nor ceasing, for it is free from conceptual discrimination.
Having practiced the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, one has already realized that external objects do not truly exist and that there is only the internal mind.
Now, one contemplates the characteristics of this internal mind and seeks it, yet finds it utterly unobtainable; therefore, it cannot be seen. This is precisely...
Emptiness pervades the ten directions horizontally; thus it is complete and immovable. It exhausts the three periods of time vertically;
thus it neither comes nor goes. This is the "provisional" (假). Its essence is the Dharmakāya, eternally abiding within the Dharma-realm;

thus its original nature is neither born nor extinguished, and it is free from conceptual discrimination. This is the "middle" (中). A single thought-moment of the inner mind is, by its very nature, a phenomenon produced through causes and conditions.
Contemplating them as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle, there is not a single thing that is not principle; therefore, it is called the contemplation of *śamatha*.
This contemplation is universally able to cease the three delusions, universally able to halt the three objects, and universally does not discriminate between cessation and non-cessation;
for this reason, it is also called the "Sublime Cessation of the Three Minds. △ Second, *vipaśyanā*.
One who practices the contemplation of the mind through the cultivation of faith visualizes internal and external forms as arising with the mind and ceasing with the mind.
This applies even up to the visualization of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*): it likewise arises with the mind and ceases with the mind.

It is like an illusion, like a transformation, like the moon reflected in water, or like an image in a mirror; it is not the mind, yet it is not separate from the mind; it does not come, nor does it not come.
It is not departing, nor is it not departing; it is not arising, nor is it not arising; it is not acting, nor is it not acting.
First, one knows that the objective realm is mind-only; furthermore, one knows that this mind is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Internal form arises following the mind. If one wishes to conceive of the cessation of internal form, then internal form ceases following the mind.

If one wishes to conceive of the arising and cessation of external form, it is likewise so. This mind is like a mirror: when the forms and images of the ten realms encounter it, they appear immediately, yet there is no coming or going.

Since the mind is fundamentally formless, the forms of each of the ten realms are individually not the mind; yet because the mind possesses form, the forms of the ten realms are all inseparable from the mind.
Since there is no form outside the mind, the forms of the ten realms have never come into being. Because the mind arises, form arises. Therefore...

It is fundamentally not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects. How, then, could it be seen, heard, sensed, or known?
Even if there were something visible, audible, sensible, or cognizable, that would not be the nature of mind, because the mind does not know itself, and the mind does not see itself.
Furthermore, one must not separately identify an object that cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
This is because it is the nature of the mind. Therefore, it is said that it is forever free from all conceptualizations of discrimination. Why is this?
Although the nature of the mind cannot be seen, heard, perceived, or known, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are themselves the substance of the mind.
One cannot separately designate a realm of not seeing, not hearing, not perceiving, and not knowing as being the mind. △ Second, clarifying what is transcended.

Gradually, one is able to transcend the meditative states of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as well as other signs of meditative objects, thereby attaining the semblance of the samādhi of emptiness.

In the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), one cultivates this true observation of *tathatā* (suchness), directly observing the nature of the mind and forever departing from conceptual discrimination.
Thus, even without studying the sequential gates of dhyāna, one is naturally able to gradually transcend the states of the four formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*).

This is because those states of the four formless concentrations are all incapable of abandoning conceptual discrimination. For instance, one who enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) must first...
Feeling weary of the cage of form, one cultivates insight to break through form and enters meditative absorption by taking infinite space as the object.
The concentrated mind corresponds with that sphere of space; abiding in this awareness is a conceptualized perception (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*), not a non-conceptual state.

Next, regarding entry into the concentration of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana-samādhi*): one must first feel weary of empty space, relinquish space, and take consciousness as the object to enter meditative absorption.
The concentrated mind is associated with that sphere of consciousness; dwelling therein, it is still a form of conceptualization and not non-conceptual.

Next, entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness—also called the sphere of non-existence—one must first cultivate weariness toward consciousness, relinquish the object of consciousness, and enter absorption by focusing on nothingness. The concentrated mind is associated with that sphere of nothingness.
This corresponds to the sphere [of neither-perception-nor-non-perception]. Abiding here and possessing this awareness is also a form of conceptualization; it is not non-conceptual.
Next, one who enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception must first cultivate weariness toward the sphere of nothingness.

Having relinquished the perception of nothingness, they enter the absorption by taking neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object. The concentrated mind and that [state of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
It is associated with the sphere of perception (*saṃjñā-vihāra*). Abiding in this subtle discernment is still a conceptualization; it is not non-conceptual.

Therefore, when the retribution is exhausted, one falls back again and does not realize the true permanence. Now, by practicing the true contemplation of Suchness (*tathatā*), one is forever free from all conceptual thoughts.
Thus, within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), one has already successfully transcended the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
One attains the gateway to the semblance *śūnyatā-samādhi*. △ Third, the accomplishment of contemplation:
When the semblance *śūnyatā-samādhi* is attained, the coarse discriminative marks of consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations do not manifest before one.
From this point onward, through diligent cultivation and study, one is protected and nurtured by spiritual friends who possess great compassion; therefore, one is freed from all hindrances.
Without obstruction, they diligently practice without ceasing, progressively entering the *citta-śānti-samādhi* (samādhi of mental tranquility).

Once they have ascended to the first stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), they are able to perfectly subdue the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsana-kleśa*). Consequently, the coarse marks of discrimination within the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) no longer manifest before them.
All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇa-mitra*), likewise [accord with them].
Guard it so that it may be nurtured and developed, until one is able to enter the samādhi of mental tranquility (*citta-śānti*).

Because one enters this samādhi by contemplating that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished, it is called "mental tranquility. When the mind is tranquil, form (*rūpa*) is also tranquil.

This concludes the initial correct demonstration of the gate of contemplation. II. The Further Advancement upon Accomplishing Contemplation. This section has two parts: first, entering realization; second, departing from faults.
Now, first:
having attained this samādhi, one is immediately able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.

Having entered this *ekavyūha-samādhi*, one beholds countless Buddhas and gives rise to a mind of profound and vast practice, abiding in the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*). That is to say, regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*...
The two types of contemplative paths of *vipaśyanā* involve resolute faith and understanding, and the ability to resolutely advance toward [enlightenment].
With the stilling of both mind and form, one reaches the end of the five stages (*pañca-varga*). The *ekavyūha-samādhi* marks the beginning of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Since the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) has reached its culmination and a semblance of understanding (*sādṛśya-adhimukti*) has arisen, it is said that "one is then able to enter. As for the term "one practice" (*ekavyūha*), it refers to the Perfect [Teaching].
Faith in the perfect understanding: one practice is all practices, and all practices are one practice.
This is what is called "binding the conditions to the Dharma-realm" and "the single thought-moment of the Dharma-realm. Since the Dharma-realm has no exterior, there are no further practices;

because it is identical with emptiness, it is called the Perfect Holy Practice (*brahmacarya*). Because it is identical with the provisional, it is called the Perfect Brahma Practice and the Practice of Infancy and Sickness. Because it is identical with the Middle Way...
This is called the "Perfect Celestial Conduct. Furthermore, because phenomena are identical to principle, the mind as a single unity perfectly possesses the conduct of the noble and Brahma heavens;
because essence is identical to function, the mind as a single unity perfectly gives rise to the conduct of an infant and the conduct of illness.

Moreover, entering the Samādhi of One Practice is precisely the previously explained clear understanding of *śamatha* and the contemplation of the mind, wherein one sees countless Buddhas and gives rise to a mind that initiates profound and vast practices—this is precisely what was previously [described].

Clearly understand the contemplation of the mind through *vipaśyanā*. By means of this single-minded, perfect, and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one abides within the stage of pure faith of the six sense faculties.

This is merely termed "definitive faith-understanding" (*niyata-adhimukti*), wherein one is definitively able to direct the mind toward the Great Bodhicitta of the One Vehicle and ascend to the Perfect Abiding (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*).
