From the Perfect Abiding upward, it is then termed "true *śamatha*."
This is because of the path of *vipaśyanā*. △ Second, the elimination of faults:
In accordance with whatever worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and samādhis he practices and studies, he has no attachment or delight in them;

even as he universally cultivates all roots of goodness and factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), he feels no fear or cowardice within saṃsāra, nor does he take pleasure in the two vehicles (*yāna*).

Within the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are still two types of persons. The first are those who practice direct, sudden contemplation (*dun guan*), flowing into the middle of the middle.
The second are those who practice either gradual or indeterminate contemplations, illuminating both sides simultaneously. Although they illuminate both sides, [they do so]...
Constantly accords with the Middle Way. Therefore, when practicing worldly *dhyāna* and *samādhi*, one does not share the ordinary person’s attachment to existence;

when cultivating the supramundane factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one does not share the two vehicles’ delight in emptiness. The successful advancement through the two contemplations is concluded.
△ Third, the concluding summary of the function of the contemplation.

Because it relies upon the most subtle and skillful means of the mind directed toward the two contemplations of cultivation, and because it is the basis for all wisdom and the root of practice, this true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) is clarified as being the most subtle and skillful means of the mind directed toward the two contemplations of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
By relying on this, one achieves the threefold wisdom within a single mind; therefore, it is the basis for all wisdom.

Relying upon this, the five practices and the myriad practices arise; therefore, it is the root of all practice. The second part, the detailed explanation of the two contemplations, is concluded. △ Third, the critical analysis.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice and study with the aforementioned faith and understanding, there are two types of persons. What are these two? First, those of sharp faculties;

second, those of dull faculties. As for those of sharp faculties, they have already been able to know that all external objects are merely the products of the mind, deceptive and unreal, like dreams or illusions, and they possess no doubt or uncertainty regarding this. [They are free from] the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-nīvaraṇa*).
Those whose [afflictions] are slight and whose distracted minds are minimal should immediately study the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness).
As for those of dull faculties who have not yet realized that all external objects are merely mind— being deceptive and unreal— and whose attachment is deep,
whose hindrances arise frequently, and whose minds are difficult to subdue, they should first study "mind-only consciousness."
Contemplation:
Although one may cultivate faith and understanding based on the single reality of the objective realm, all such individuals belong to the stage of "names" within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Yet, among these practitioners of the Perfect Teaching, there are still those of sharp and dull faculties. If one has long cultivated perfect understanding and realizes that the objective realm is nothing but mind, [one overcomes] the habitual tendencies of the five turbidities.
As for those of lesser capacity, their hindrances are slight and their distractions are few;

thus they are able to realize that the mind of consciousness is fundamentally quiescent, and to understand that the three thousand realms are, in their very suchness, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This is called practicing the true contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
However, if one has only recently attained perfect hearing, yet defiled attachments remain thick and the habits of the five turbidities are heavy, then the hindrances will be obstructive.

Thoughts arise frequently, and the mind is difficult to subdue; therefore, one must observe the arising of the mind as it transforms and creates the ten realms, knowing that there is nothing that is not itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This is called first training in the contemplation of consciousness-only.
However, those of dull faculties cannot immediately practice the contemplation of true suchness, whereas those of sharp faculties may do so without hindrance.

The contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*) merely subsumes phenomena under principle; thus it is called the "contemplation of the reality of suchness" (*tathatā-bhūta-darśana*).
When one enters principle by means of phenomena, it is simply termed the "contemplation of mind-only consciousness.

If one were to abandon phenomena to contemplate principle alone, it would be neither the contemplation of mind-only consciousness nor the contemplation of the reality of suchness. For this reason, the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* strictly warns beginners against such an approach.

One must not bypass the first two natures and proceed directly to practice based on the third nature; rather, one should study all three aspects concurrently within every moment of thought to support the completion of the third aspect.

According to this principle, during the stage of the name (nāma-pada), one may only first practice the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti-darśana*), because at that stage one is still unable to prevent the arising of the minds of the nine realms. This refers to the initial grade of the stage of contemplative practice (*darśana-pratipatti*).
One may then practice these two contemplations according to one’s inclination. When the mind of the nine realms arises, one contemplates consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*);
when the mind of the nine realms does not arise, one contemplates true suchness (*tathatā*). When contemplating consciousness-only, form is quiescent and the mind is likewise quiescent;
when contemplating true suchness, the mind is quiescent and form is likewise quiescent. This concludes the initial correct elucidation of the two contemplations. △

The second section, concerning the conditions for obstacles, has three parts: first, manifesting the conditions for leaving obstacles; second, seeking birth in the Pure Land; third, concluding with praise of the skillful means.

Within the first of these, there are three sections: first, clarifying the conditions for obstacles; second, demonstrating the skillful means; third, clarifying the attainment of freedom from obstacles. This is the first [of those three].
If a person, though they study and possess such faith and understanding, has weak roots of goodness and karma, they will be unable to advance.
Their various evil afflictions cannot be gradually subdued; their minds become doubtful and timid, fearing they will fall into the three evil realms or be born in the eight difficult states.

They fear that they will not constantly encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, nor be able to make offerings or hear and receive the True Dharma. They fear that the practice of bodhi will be difficult to accomplish.

Accomplishment. Those who possess such doubts, fears, and various obstacles, even though they study and cultivate such faith and understanding—meaning they study and cultivate faith and understanding based on the single, ultimate reality—are still merely people at the initial stage of the name.
Because their pure habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are shallow, their roots of goodness and karma are meager; because their defiled habitual tendencies are thick, [they remain hindered].
If the afflictions are not subdued, this must be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). There are those whose roots of goodness are thick while their afflictions are thin;
these are the ones who, as mentioned before, should immediately practice the true contemplation of *tathatā*. There are those whose roots of goodness are thick while their afflictions are also thick;
these are the ones who, as mentioned before, should first practice the contemplation of consciousness-only (*cittamātra-vijñaptimātra*). If...
Regarding the case where both the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are thin: this situation allows for two directions.

Because the afflictions are thin, one may practice the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness); because the roots of goodness are thin, one may first study the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
Now, for those whose roots of goodness are thin while their afflictions are thick, they possess much doubt and many obstacles, and thus cannot immediately practice [the contemplation of suchness].
Regarding the contemplation of mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), it is necessary to specifically demonstrate skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). II. Demonstrating Skillful Means (in three parts):
1. Invoking the Name; 2. Contemplating the Dharma-body; 3. Cultivating Disgust and Detachment.

Invoking the Name refers to employing the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—specifically its pure aspect (*viśuddha-bhāga*)—to assist the contemplation of mind-consciousness alone (*citta-mātra-vijñāna-darśana*), thereby counteracting the notion of impermanence.

Encountering the fear of hearing the Dharma from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one who contemplates the Dharma-body employs the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the true nature of the pure portion to assist in the contemplation of *tathatā*,
thereby counteracting the fear that the practices for awakening (*bodhicaryā*) are difficult to accomplish.
One who cultivates revulsion (*nirveda*) correctly destroys the two natures— the imagined and the dependent— which belong to the defiled portion, thereby accomplishing "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).

This is the first [section], which concerns the gradual subduing of afflictions through the contemplation of consciousness and the counteracting of the fears of the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions.
At all times and in all places, one should constantly and diligently recite and keep my name in mind.
The true merits, general and specific names, and titles of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arise from the realization of true nature (*tathatā*).

These are the functioning of conditions produced in accordance with that nature, capable of acting as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings. Yet, sentient beings do not understand this.
If one conceives of the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as existing externally to the mind, this is subsumed under the pure aspect of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

If one knows that these names and titles are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by one’s own mind, they are subsumed under the pure aspect of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
If one can constantly and diligently recite and contemplate them at all times and in all places without interruption, the mind will not become distracted; this is called...

Exquisite stillness (śamatha) has its name clearly established; it is called "exquisite contemplation" (vipaśyanā). This can assist in manifesting the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, while simultaneously possessing the superior function of extinguishing hindrances. △ Second, the contemplation of the Dharma-body.
If one attains single-mindedness, one's roots of goodness will increase and one's resolve will become sharp and powerful.
One should then contemplate that my Dharma-body, as well as the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas, are equal in essence to one’s own body—non-dual and undifferentiated, neither arising nor ceasing.
Permanent, blissful, self, and pure; with perfected merit and virtue, this is worthy of taking refuge as a source of reliance.
If one attains single-mindedness and causes roots of goodness to increase, it is due to having diligently recited the name at all times and in all places as previously described.

This means prostrating to eliminate dullness and distraction. Once dullness and distraction are eliminated, the mind becomes sharp and vigorous, capable of relying upon the single true realm to cultivate faith and understanding.
One observes that the Great Being Kṣitigarbha and all Buddhas alike have realized this present, single thought of the self-nature pure *tathāgatagarbha* as the *dharmakāya*. My own body...
Furthermore, it takes the Tathāgatagarbha, which is intrinsically pure by nature, as its very substance.
Although delusion and awakening differ, their nature is eternally equal. Sentient beings and Buddhas are nothing other than this single mind; therefore, they are not two.

Since there is no separation or distinction based on delusion or awakening, they are not separate. Having been accomplished from time immemorial, they are unborn; being eternally and perpetually abiding, they are thus [unchanging].
It is unextinguished; because it is without counterpart, it is eternal. Because it has nothing received, it is blissful. Because it is free from conceptual proliferation, it is the self.
Because there is nothing to be abandoned, it is pure. Thus, the inconceivable, untainted, and pure karma inherent in its nature is ultimately and fully manifested.
Thus, when merit is perfected, one takes refuge in the Great Being and the Buddha; this is entirely taking refuge in one's own mind.

Therefore, it is said: "One takes refuge in oneself as the Buddha, one takes refuge in oneself as the Dharma, and one takes refuge in oneself as the Sangha. Apart from this self-Dharma, there is nothing else.
Furthermore, where else could there be three jewels distinct from these to which one might take refuge?
All who take refuge in the Three Jewels—whether they have attained realization or not—are, in ultimate truth, taking refuge in themselves alone. △ Third, cultivating renunciation.

Furthermore, one observes the characteristics of one's own body and mind as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; they are like illusions and transformations, and thus should be viewed with revulsion and detachment.
The nature of the mind in this present moment is fundamentally identical in essence to that of the Great Beings and all Buddhas;

yet, due to delusion since beginningless time, one has falsely identified the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body and falsely identified the reflected shadows of the six sense objects as the characteristics of one's own mind.

It is like discarding the ocean to recognize only the bubbles; how could one fail to falsely perceive impermanence within the eternally abiding, to experience suffering within happiness, to lack sovereignty within the nature of sovereignty, and to falsely construct defilement within the nature of purity?
Furthermore, this false body and false mind—characterized by impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—arise based upon the single thought-moment of the present mind-nature.
They are merely like illusions and transformations; they possess no separate reality.
Why, then, are you deluded by this deceptive and unsubstantial body and mind, giving rise to various evil afflictions? Cultivate this sense of weary detachment as an antidote.
By discerning and detaching from attachments, one is able to accomplish the two kinds of contemplative paths. This concludes the second section, showing the skillful means.
△ Third, clarifying the attainment of detachment:
If one can practice and study such contemplation, the mind of pure faith will swiftly increase, and all obstacles—
It will gradually diminish. Why is this? Such a person is called one who studies hearing my name, and is likewise able to study hearing the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions;

they are called one who studies single-mindedly prostrating to and making offerings to me, and is likewise able to study single-mindedly prostrating to and making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions; they are called one who studies hearing the profound Mahāyāna.
"Sūtra" refers to those who study, uphold, transcribe, and reverently make offerings to the profound Mahāyāna sūtras;

it refers to those who study, receive, maintain, read, and recite the profound Mahāyāna sūtras; it refers to those who study to remain far removed from wrong views and do not fall into slander regarding the profound and correct meaning;
it refers to those who study and believe in the ultimate, most profound, and supreme true meaning.
One who understands this is called one capable of eliminating all karmic obstacles and one destined to attain an immeasurable mass of merit.
When such a person relinquishes the body, they shall never fall into the evil realms or the eight difficult conditions. They will again hear the True Dharma, cultivate faith, and practice it;
furthermore, they will be able to be reborn according to their vows in the pure Buddha-lands of other directions.

Practice such contemplation. This involves contemplating both the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the practice of renunciation. The single thought-moment of the present is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
By now contemplating the Dharma-body, one can manifest the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) within the dependent nature.
Furthermore, by cultivating renunciation, one can eliminate the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) within the dependent nature.
By manifesting the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature), pure faith increases; by eliminating the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), all obstacles are diminished. Why is this?

The following section praises his excellent training. Indeed, both myself and the Buddhas of the ten directions do nothing more than transform and extinguish the *parikalpita* within the *paratantra* (dependent nature), causing it to be completely purified;
and we transform and manifest the *pariniṣpanna* within the *paratantra*, causing it to...
That which is thus fulfilled is precisely this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as it is revealed here;

it is called the "Three Jewels in One Essence" (*eka-rasa triratna*), and is also termed the ultimate, profound, and foremost true meaning. Why is this? The principle of suchness (*tathatā*) is called the Jewel of Dharma;
the wisdom of suchness is called the Jewel of Buddha; and the non-duality of wisdom and principle is called the Jewel of Saṃgha. This is the full realization of their single essence.
The Three Jewels are the Buddhas of the ten directions. Those who have partially realized the single essence of the Three Jewels are the great Bodhisattvas.
Those that elucidate and manifest the single essence of the Three Jewels are the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
To hear of this single essence of the Three Jewels without doubt is called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). To observe the single essence of the Three Jewels without...

That which is free from obstruction is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). To be aware of this single essence of the Triple Gem in every thought-moment without interruption is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Now, if this practitioner can single-mindedly recite the name while contemplating the Dharma-body and wearying of deluded attachments, then upon hearing the great name of Kṣitigarbha, it is as if they have heard the names of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions; they shall offer worship and make offerings.
To nourish Kṣitigarbha is equivalent to universally prostrating to and making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

It may be said that even if the Buddha does not preach the Dharma, one constantly hears his Brahma-voice; though no sound of speech issues from the mouth, one recites all the scriptures; though no scroll is held in the hand, one constantly expounds this sutra;
and though the mind does not engage in discursive thought, it universally illumines the Dharma-realm. What karmic obstacles could there be that would not be eliminated? What...
How could there be any merit that remains unfulfilled? What gates to the evil realms would not be closed? And what pure Buddha-lands would there be where one would not be reborn?
This concludes the first section: Manifesting the Conditions for Leaving Obstructions. II. Seeking Rebirth in a Pure Land.

Furthermore, if there are those who wish to be born in a pure land currently existing in another direction, they should single-mindedly recite and keep in mind the name of the Buddha of that world, with focused attention and without distraction. For one who observes as described above, it is certain that they will be born in that Buddha’s pure land;
their roots of goodness will increase, and they will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression.

The preceding passage has already clarified that those who seek to be free from obstacles cultivate three expedient means; not only do they thereby eliminate all obstacles in the present life, but they can also be reborn according to their vows.

Now, we shall specifically clarify that for those who seek birth in the Pure Land, if they can cultivate these three expedient means, they will not only certainly attain birth in the Pure Land, but will also be able to achieve non-retrogression in the present life. This is achieved by reciting and chanting with single-minded devotion.
The name of that Buddha causes one to leave behind dullness and distraction; this is precisely what is meant by "single-mindedness without confusion. This is the expedient means of invoking the Name.
Observing as described above constitutes the two expedient means of contemplating the Dharma-body and cultivating revulsion [for saṃsāra].

When these three expedient means are complete, one will certainly be reborn in that land after casting off the body. One's present roots of goodness will increase, and one will swiftly attain [the stage of non-retrogression].

[The practitioner] regresses. Therefore, one should know that the practice of holding the Name possesses great merit; it must not be regarded as a shallow or mundane teaching. △ Third, the conclusion and praise of the skillful means, which has two parts:

first, praising the superiority of the karma of single-mindedness; second, distinguishing that the benefit of distracted and confused practice is slight. The first part [praising the superiority of the karma of single-mindedness] further has two sections:
first, the actual praise; second, the concluding explanation. Now, the first [the actual praise]:
One should know that among all roots of goodness, the practice of single-mindedly binding one's mindfulness to contemplate the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas is the most supreme karmic activity.
Specifically, for those who diligently cultivate this, they will gradually be able to advance toward the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi).
If one attains the *ekavyūha-samādhi*, then a vast and subtle mind of practice is perfected; this is called "attaining a semblance of non-arising."
Dharma-patience:
based upon the single reality realm, one opens up the perfect understanding that the Buddhas of the ten directions, myself, and all sentient beings share the same pure mind as their essence;
this is called "one mind. To constantly and diligently recite the names of the Buddhas is [the practice].
Fixing the mind, one contemplates that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is equal to one’s own.
This is called contemplating the equality of the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas; among all roots of goodness, this is the most supreme. Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:
It is not by means of small roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit that one can be born in that land.

By upholding the Name for one day up to seven days with a single mind and without distraction, one immediately attains rebirth there. It is through this very act of upholding the Name that this is achieved.
This is precisely because of the causes and conditions of many roots of goodness and merit.

The preceding section clarified that those who cultivate the two contemplations must first attain the samādhis of the tranquility of form and the tranquility of mind before they can enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
Now, by fixing the mind upon the name, one should practice the contemplation of mind-only; by contemplating the Dharma-body, one should practice the contemplation of true suchness. Therefore...
This is precisely how one approaches the *ekavyūha-samādhi*. To comprehend the single mind while reciting the name—such is its efficacy.
How can one not believe it?
For by being able to hear my name, one is likewise able to hear the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one is able...
Because they have wholeheartedly paid homage and made offerings to me; because they are also able to wholeheartedly pay homage and make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
because they are able to hear the profound Mahāyāna sūtras; because they are able to uphold, transcribe, make offerings to, and revere the profound Mahāyāna sūtras;
and because they are able to receive, maintain, read, and recite the profound Mahāyāna sūtras; they are able [to dwell] within the ultimate profundity.
In the ultimate reality, one does not give rise to fear; being free from slander, one attains a mind of right view through the power of faith and understanding.
Because it definitively eliminates all karmic obstructions and because one directly realizes an immeasurable mass of merit.
This means that by means of perfect hearing, perfect reflection, and perfect cultivation, one is able to reach the Samādhi of One Practice.
Hearing my name, hearing the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and hearing the profound Mahāyāna sūtras—this refers to the wisdom of hearing within the stage of names and words.

With a sincere heart, they pay homage and make offerings to me and all Buddhas; they uphold, read, and recite the profound Mahāyāna sūtras without giving rise to fear, thereby attaining a mind of right view—this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

They decisively eliminate karmic obstacles and manifest immeasurable merit—this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*). △ Second, the conclusion.
Why is this? It is because the non-conceptual bodhicitta manifests as tranquil wisdom, giving rise to the various vows and practices of skillful means and activity.
Those who are able to hear my name attain the practice of definitive faith and benefit;
even all those who are capable [of hearing it] shall attain the cause of the non-retrogressive One Vehicle.
Non-conceptual bodhicitta is the mind that has faith and understanding in the single reality of the ultimate realm.
The manifestation of tranquil wisdom is the practice of faith in the contemplation of *śamatha*.

The arousal of various vows and practices as skillful means is the practice of faith in the contemplation of *vipaśyanā*. Only by attaining decisive faith in beneficial conduct does one become truly capable.
By hearing my name, one obtains the cause for non-retrogression in the One Vehicle; only then can one truly perform all possible acts such as wholehearted prostration.
This concludes the first section, which praises the excellence of the karma of single-minded devotion. II. Distinguishing from Confused Benefits that are Subtle (This has two parts):
A. Hearing yet not hearing; B. Cultivating yet not cultivating. Now, the first part: Hearing yet not hearing.
If one’s mind is distracted and defiled, even though they recite my name, it cannot be called "hearing" [the Dharma], because they are unable to give rise to resolute faith and understanding;
they will merely obtain worldly rewards of merit, but shall not attain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits.
Failing to realize that there are no phenomena external to the mind is called "confusion. When one's own mind turns back to grasp its own mind, it is called "distraction.
To falsely give rise to various forms of defiled attachment is called "impurity.

Therefore, although one may recite [the name], one does not achieve true hearing, because one has not yet heard the true meaning of the two characters "Earth-Treasury" (Dizang). "Earth" is the mind-ground; "Treasury" is...
The Dharma-nature treasury: the nature of the mind is non-dual; how could there be admixture? Since it is fundamentally without admixture, by what means could there be disorder?

Since there is already no disorder, how could there be defilement? Now, because they do not realize this non-dual nature of the mind, they falsely construct the obstacles of admixture, disorder, and defilement within that which is fundamentally free from admixture, disorder, and defilement. This is because they have not heard the perfect name of the Earth Store (Kṣitigarbha). If...
Within the stage of names, wisdom arises from hearing the single reality of the ultimate realm in its entirety; thus, the mind is free from confusion.
Within the stage of contemplative practice, wisdom arises from contemplating the true suchness of consciousness-only in its entirety; thus, the mind is free from distraction.
Next, within the stage of semblance, wisdom arises from cultivating the samādhi of one practice in its entirety; thus, the mind...

When free from defilement, one achieves resolute faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). Nevertheless, even if one recites the name with a distracted or defiled mind, one will still obtain various worldly wholesome rewards;
namely, one is freed from decline and affliction in the present life, and is reborn among humans or devas in future lives.
Through gradual cultivation and habituation, one will ultimately attain the Buddha-way. However, one cannot immediately obtain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits in this very life.
It is merely a burden. △ Second, practicing as if not practicing:
Such a distracted and defiled mind cannot attain profound and great benefit from any of the various virtues it practices.
This intends to clarify that if one opens up the perfect understanding (yuanjie), then whatever wholesome practices one cultivates will all yield great benefit. This is what is meant by the saying:

"When a person of the Perfect Teaching receives the Dharma, there is no dharma that is not perfect. Second, the demonstration of the two kinds of contemplative paths to reveal the perfect practice is concluded.

△ Third, the demonstration of the three patiences and four Buddhas to manifest the perfect stages has three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; third, the differentiation.
First, regarding cultivation:
Good son, you should know that those who diligently cultivate and study signless dhyāna as described above will, before long, be able to obtain profound and great benefits,
and will gradually become Buddhas.
"Signless Dhyāna" refers to the two types of contemplation—*vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and *tathatā* (suchness)—cultivated based on the single reality realm.
These two types of contemplation are called "signless" because they are devoid of the signs of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the signs of nirvāṇa.

They are called "dhyāna" because they fully possess both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as well as concentration and wisdom. The Sanskrit term for dhyāna is *dhyāna*, which is translated here as "meditative concentration" (*靜慮*).
"Quietude" (jing) refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding); "contemplation" (lü) refers to *vipaśyanā* (insight). These are also alternative names for "tranquility and illumination.
"Profound and great benefit" refers to the adornment of merit; "gradually becoming a Buddha" refers to the adornment of wisdom.

Furthermore, "benefit" pertains to patience (*kṣānti*) and the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while "becoming a Buddha" pertains to wisdom and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). △ Second, the specific [explanation].

The second section [of the first part] has two parts: first, the explanation of the benefit; second, the explanation of becoming a Buddha. The first [of these two] also has two parts: first, clarifying the entry into the stage; second, explaining the meaning of "patience" (*kṣānti*). Now, for the first:

regarding the profound and great benefit, it refers to attaining entry into the stage of the dharma-position of firm faith (*adhimukti-dharmatā-sthiti*), thereby accomplishing the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*). Thus, one enters the stage of firmness.

The stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) is so called because one achieves the conforming patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Upon entering the stage of correct reality (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one achieves the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The ten minds of initial aspiration (*prathama-cittotpāda*) are called the patience of firm faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*); the ten minds of nurturing (*puṣṭi-citta*) are called the patience of firm dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*);

and the ten adamantine minds (*vajra-citta*) are called the patience of firm cultivation (*bhāvanā-kṣānti*). Now, these are collectively termed the "stage of firm cultivation. Their essential nature consists of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), which are called the "Non-" [referring to *asaṃskṛta* or *anabhilāpya*].

Birth-endurance (*janma-kṣānti*). Partially realizing the Dharma-body is called entering the Bodhisattva’s correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*). However, the various sutras clarify patience (*kṣānti*) with varying degrees of expansion and contraction;

furthermore, there are differences between the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as between horizontal and vertical classifications. Now, I must briefly analyze these to demonstrate their general principles.
Furthermore, one must establish the names according to their meaning so that they do not overlap; this is done through three intentions: first, listing the names; second, explaining them;

and third, assigning them to their respective categories. First, regarding the listing of names: some clarify two types of patience (*kṣānti*), namely, first, patience regarding arising (*utpatti-kṣānti*), and second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*).

Alternatively, it clarifies three patiences (*kṣānti*), as in this text. Alternatively, it clarifies four patiences: first, the patience of subduing (*avaivartika-kṣānti*); second, the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); third, the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*);
and fourth, the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*). Alternatively, it clarifies five patiences by adding the second, the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).

Alternatively, it clarifies six patiences by adding the third, the patience of harmonious compliance (*samanujñā-kṣānti*), which serves as the fourth [in that sequence]. Second, the explanation is brief.
Taking the endurance of resentment and harm as "patience toward beings" (*sattvakṣānti*) and the endurance of diligent toil as "patience toward dharmas" (*dharmakṣānti*) is not what is intended here.

Nor is it what is intended when the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdeśanā) designates the stages prior to the [first] ground as patience toward beings—being shallow—and the stages from the first ground upward as patience toward dharmas—being deep.

The Perfect Teaching (*Pariniṣpannadeśanā*) clarifies that because the provisional names of the ten realms are all empty, this constitutes patience toward beings; and because the real dharmas of the ten realms are all... [empty].

Because it is empty, it constitutes the patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*). One observes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividhaśūnyatā*) perfectly; there is no sequence and no gradation of depth. Regarding the three patiences:

in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the patience of faith (*kṣānti-śraddhā*); the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) constitute the conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*); and ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) constitutes the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-vyavasthāna*), from beginning to end, one believes in the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*); all are termed the patience of faith. From beginning to end, one is in accord with reality.

When appearances do not contradict one another, they are all termed "patience in accordance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). When neither at the beginning nor at the end does one give rise to a mind of the two extremes, it is all termed "patience in non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the four types of patience: according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute "submissive patience" (*vinaya-kṣānti*);

"patience in accordance" and "patience in non-arising" are as previously explained; and "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is termed "patience in quiescent extinction" (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). According to the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), from the initial mind up to...

In the *Vajraśekhara*, all [stages] that completely subdue the five abodes of delusion are termed "Patience in Subduing" (*kṣānti*). Both the initial and final stages are entirely the cessation of all practices;
thus they are collectively termed "Patience in Quiescence" (*śānti-kṣānti*). "Conformity" (*anuloma*) and "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are as previously explained. Regarding the five types of patience:

in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), the initial mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is taken as "subduing," while the final mind is taken as "faith. "Conformity" and so forth are as before. In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*), [the same applies].

This is also as previously explained. Regarding the six types of patience (*kṣānti*): in the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), the ten abodes (*bhūmi*) are divided into "conformity" (*anuloma*) and "following" (*anuśrava*).

The ten practices (*caryā*) and ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute "accordance. In the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), from beginning to end there is no deviation from the true mark (*dharmatā*);

thus, all may be termed "conformity and following. As for the three categories of connection: the words of the present sutra are restrictive in scope while the intent is universal; it does not distinguish between two, three, or four patiences.
Regarding the five patiences and six patiences: all the various patiences within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) are grouped together as "Patience of Faith" (*kṣānti-śraddhā*).
All the various patiences within the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*) are grouped together as "Conformity Patience" (*anuloma-kṣānti*).

All the various patiences from the stage of partial realization up to the ultimate stage are grouped together as "Patience of Non-arising" (*anutpāda-kṣānti*). △ Second, the explanation of the meaning of patience.

Furthermore, those who have accomplished the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) are able to act as the lineage of the Tathāgata; those who have accomplished the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) are able to understand the conduct of the Tathāgata;
and those who have accomplished the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) attain the activity of the Tathāgata.

The sublime concentration that serves as the basis for the Tathāgata’s untainted wisdom is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Relying upon this patience, one gives rise to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and acts as the seed of a Tathāgata;
therefore, it is named "faith-patience" (*śraddhākṣānti*). Relying upon this patience, one gives rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*).

Understanding the conduct of the Tathāgata is called "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti). Relying upon this patience, one gives rise to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and attains the activity of a Tathāgata;
this is called "non-arising patience" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). It is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet it can be both horizontal and vertical. Vertically, it is categorized into three stages.
This is a horizontal overview of the single mind. The first section, the explanation of "benefit," is concluded. △ Second, the explanation of "becoming a Buddha.
Regarding the gradual attainment of Buddhahood, there are briefly four types. What are these four? First, becoming a Buddha through the fulfillment of faith in the Dharma.
This refers to relying on the stage of the seed-nature (*gotrabhūmi*), wherein one gains definitive faith that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, and are pure and level.
1. Because there is nothing further to be wished for or sought. 2. Because one attains Buddhahood through the fulfillment of understanding the Dharma;

that is to say, by relying on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one deeply understands the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), knows that the activities of the Tathāgata are without creation or fabrication, and does not give rise to dualistic conceptions regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, because the mind is free from fear.
3. Because one attains Buddhahood through the fulfillment of realization of the Dharma; that is to say, by relying on the stage of the pure mind (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*).
Because they have attained the non-conceptual, tranquil knowledge of dharmas and inconceivable, spontaneous activity, and because they are free from the notion of seeking;
fourth, because all meritorious practices are fulfilled, they become Buddhas— meaning that by relying on the ultimate Bodhisattva stage,
they are able to eliminate all hindrances, as the dreams of ignorance are exhausted.

The fulfillment of the Dharma refers to the perfect, non-conceptual Dharma of the single reality realm (*ekasatya-dharmadhātu*). Because of fulfilling the Dharma through faith, one is a Buddha in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

Because of fulfilling the Dharma through understanding, one is a Buddha in the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa*). Because of fulfilling the Dharma through realization, one is a Buddha in the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*).
Because their meritorious practices are fulfilled, they ultimately become Buddhas. Since their nature is eternally equal, all are called Buddhas;

yet because their cultivation is either clear or obscure, it is said that there are four [stages]. This is the gradual approach within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjia), wherein the gradual is none other than the perfect. This is the "Six Identities" (Liujijie) of Tiantai.
It is fundamentally based on this. It is a dharma-gate that eliminates pride and eliminates timidity, perfecting both beauty and goodness. Part Two: The Separate Explanations are concluded.
△ Part Three: Distinguishing the Cultivation. This has two sections: First, distinguishing three types of persons; Second, showing ten kinds of characteristics. Now, the first section.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are three types of those who practice and study worldly meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with signs. What are these three?
First, because they lack the power of skillful means and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), they greedily grasp at the merits of various dhyāna-samādhis and give rise to arrogance;
thus bound by their dhyāna, they regress and seek after the mundane world. Second, because they lack the power of skillful means and resolute conviction, they rely upon dhyāna...
Third, there are those who, possessing the power of skillful means and resolute faith— namely,
by relying on the single reality realm and practicing the two paths of observation, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—
are able to resolve that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions, being like dreams and illusions. Although...
They attain the merits of all worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) yet do not cling to them firmly; they no longer regress to seek the fruits of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Furthermore, because they believe and know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, they are neither terrified nor daunted, and thus do not regress to seek the vehicles of the two [lesser] vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The preceding section clarified the cultivation of supramundane signless meditation (*animitta-dhyāna*), by which one can swiftly accomplish the three patiences (*kṣānti*) and the four fruits of Buddhahood.
Now, to distinguish the cultivation and study of mundane meditation with signs (*sanimitta-dhyāna*), there are three types of distinctions.

It is intended that people first study the Mahāyāna as a skillful means for advancement, cultivating faith and understanding based upon the single reality (*ekasatya*) of the objective realm, so as not to err.

This refers to falling into the world or the two vehicles. To speak of "having signs" (sanimitta) means the twelve gates of dhyāna—namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments—all of which have objective signs (*ālambana*) that can be grasped.

To greedily receive these various dhyānas and thereby give rise to arrogance is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride). Having only just suppressed the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) in the desire realm, one still gives rise to [afflictions] in the higher realms.
Regarding the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-vicāra*): although one is temporarily freed from the bonds of desire, one remains bound by the bonds of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Consequently, one becomes remote from Bodhi and regresses to seek the pleasurable retributions of the worldly realms of form and formlessness. This refers to practitioners who, relying on meditative concentration, give rise to a practice of partial revulsion and detachment;
that is, because they have realized the first dhyāna and so forth, they observe the faults and afflictions of the three realms with a concentrated mind and perceive the suffering of birth and death.
They sever the accumulation of afflictions, rejoice in the cessation of nirvana, and cultivate the path of eternal detachment; they no longer give rise to the skillful means of great compassion.

If one relies on the single reality-realm as the primary skillful means and practices the non-dual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of calm abiding and insight, then one will know that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions. All [phenomena]...
Like a dream or an illusion, its very substance is unreal. How can one allow firm attachment or fearful dread to arise toward such phenomena as dreams and illusions?

Thus we know that those who lack skillful means and resolute faith become attached to various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), thereby producing the characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃsāra*);
or, relying on these absorptions, they give rise to revulsion, thereby producing the empty characteristic of nirvāṇa. However, if one possesses skillful means and resolute faith...
One who sports within the various dhyānas is not bound by those dhyānas. That which exists as birth and death is itself the existence of the true mark (dharmatā).
One deeply contemplates nirvāṇa yet does not grasp at its realization; that which is the emptiness of nirvāṇa is itself the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
In the existence of the true mark, there is the mark of non-existence; in the emptiness of the ultimate meaning, there is the mark of non-emptiness. Thus, each and every one [is such].
All these constitute the meditation of signlessness (animitta-dhyāna). △ Second, showing the ten kinds of signs:

Those who thus practice and study all the dharmas of dhyāna and samādhi should know that there are ten sequential gates of signs which fully encompass the activity of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) and enable the practitioner to achieve realization in accordance with the truth, without error or confusion.

Error. What are the ten? This clarifies that regardless of whether one practices formless or formed meditations, one must understand these ten types of characteristic-gates (*lakṣaṇa-mukha*) before being able to achieve success without error.
If one does not grasp the meaning of these ten gates, [one remains] in the world...
Even the first dhyāna is difficult to accomplish, let alone the supramundane, most excellent dhyānas.
If one attains the intent of these ten gates, then there is no practice of meditative concentration that will not be fully encompassed, mastered, and accomplished.
First is the characteristic of the skillful means for gathering mindfulness (*samādāpana-upāya-lakṣaṇa*).
This is as explained in the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (Stopping and Seeing) regarding the twenty-five preliminary skillful means (*pūrvāṅga-upāya*).
Whether one is practicing mundane or supramundane dhyāna, all must possess these: first, possessing the five conditions; second, reviling the five desires; third, abandoning the five [hindrances].

In brief: fourth, harmonizing the five matters; fifth, practicing the five dharmas. I urge you to carefully examine such works as the *Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Mohe zhiguan) and the *Dhyāna-pāramitā-sūtra*.
Second, the desire to abide in the characteristics of objects.

This is the primary gateway of internal skillful means; that is to say, whether it be *ānāpāna-sthiti* (stopping by binding the object), *citta-nigraha-sthiti* (stopping by restraining the mind), or *tattva-darśana-sthiti* (stopping by realizing reality), each necessarily has its own observed object.
Third: Regarding the stage of the initial dwelling, one clearly and distinctly knows the signs of exiting and entering.
This is the method for beginners to settle the mind within the internal skillful means. One does not allow the mind to become dull or distracted according to the object being contemplated;
when rising or sitting, one knows the sign of exiting, and while sitting, one knows the sign of entering.
Fourth, one attains the mark of firm stability by dwelling well within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

This is the method for attaining mental tranquility (*citta-sthiti*) within the internal skillful means (*antara-upāya*). For example, one who cultivates mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) has the mind dwell well upon the inhalation and exhalation;
likewise, even one who cultivates the realization of the true nature of reality (*tattva-bhāvanā*) has the mind dwell well within all phenomena (*dharma*).
Emptiness, etc.
Fifth is the characteristic of the application of effort, wherein one vigorously applies skillful means to further seek and advance in cultivation.

For example, one who practices *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), having already attained the coarse abiding of the desire realm, further seeks the subtle abiding, and so on until the cultivation [is complete].
Regarding "realizing the true nature": one observes all phenomena through successive stages and finds that none are not empty.

Sixth, one gradually attains harmony and compliance, experiencing joy and pleasure according to one's heart; one eliminates doubt and attains faith and understanding, which is the sign of self-comfort.

For instance, one who cultivates *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) realizes the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), wherein the awakened mind is clear and pure, corresponding with meditative absorption.

The dharma of concentration sustains the mind so that there is no intention for distraction. This continues up to the practitioner who cultivates the realization of reality (*tattva-bhāvanā*), who clearly understands and resolves that all phenomena are fundamentally empty.
Seventh, one attains superior progress. Regarding that which the mind is focused upon, there arises a slight degree of correspondence and the perception of signs of benefit.

For example, in the practice of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), from the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), one enters a state of profound emptiness and openness, losing the sense of the body belonging to the desire realm, and begins to realize the eight tactile sensations (*aṣṭasparśa*) of the first dhyāna: either movement or itching, or coolness or warmth, or lightness or heaviness.
Whether it be rough or smooth, as soon as one tactile sensation arises, ten kinds of wholesome dharmas and merits arise in conjunction with it:
first, concentration; second, emptiness; third, purity; fourth, joy; fifth, bliss; sixth, the arising of a wholesome mind;
seventh, clear knowledge and vision; eighth, liberation from entanglements; ninth, the manifestation of the objective realm; and tenth, the mind becoming pliant and supple. Therefore...

This refers to the characteristic of realizing benefit through partial correspondence. Even for one who cultivates the true essence and attains the first dhyāna, they partially correspond with the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā), which constitutes the realization of benefit.
Eighth, the characteristic of the accomplishment of the antidote through further cultivation, increasing clarity, firming up what has been practiced, and attaining superior qualities.

For example, in the case of one practicing *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) who has already attained the first *dhyāna*, the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*) are accomplished: namely, first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, sustained thought (*vicāra*);

third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). Being non-retrogressive and non-deviating, it serves as the antidote to the distraction of desire and is fully complete.

One accomplishes the merits of the first dhyāna, and so on, until the practitioner who cultivates the true essence finds the principle of emptiness increasingly clarified and severs all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*).
Ninth: whatever thoughts arise in the mind, external manifestations of meritorious deeds appear in accordance with one's wishes, being consistent and free from error or delusion.

Regarding the characteristics: for instance, one who has realized the first dhyāna can produce two kinds of transformations—namely, transformations of the first dhyāna and transformations of the desire realm.

One who has realized the second dhyāna can produce three transformations; one who has realized the third dhyāna can produce four transformations; and one who has realized the fourth dhyāna... [can produce five transformations].

This refers to being able to manifest five transformations, collectively termed the fourteen transformations. Furthermore, one who has realized the true essence is able to manifest the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Tenth: if one practices differently, relying on what was previously attained to give rise to skillful means (*upāya*), they will achieve them in successive order, entering and emerging from them.
It follows the mind; it is characterized by the mastery of transcendence.

For instance, one who has realized the first dhyāna may further cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, as well as all meditative absorptions through contemplation, refinement, and cultivation;
yet there is none among them that does not arise based upon the first dhyāna already attained.
Only through skillful means can one achieve success in stages. Once success is achieved, one is able to enter and emerge according to the mind.

Having followed the mind, one is then able to transcend with mastery. Furthermore, for one who has already realized the cessation that accords with the true nature of reality (*tattva-vipaśyanā*), whether they further cultivate other skillful means such as the cessation that follows conditions (*anurūpa-vipaśyanā*), or even the cessation that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes (*anta-dvaya-vikalpa-śamana*), there is nothing that does not rely [upon this].

Having attained the true stillness of the realized essence, one gives rise to skillful means; thus, one is able to successively achieve mastery over entering and emerging at will, attaining transcendent freedom.
This is called the tenfold gate of sequential characteristics, which encompasses the practice of meditative concentration.

Even for those who cultivate the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, the contemplation of the true suchness (tathatā), or the world-transcending signless dhyāna, they must necessarily possess these ten sequential gates of characteristics before attaining accomplishment and before constantly remaining in correspondence with śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon this! Part Two: The Exposition on the Meaning of Progression is concluded. △ Three.
Demonstrating skillful exposition in two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Now, for the first:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Firm Pure Faith addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"How do you skillfully expound the profound Dharma, enabling sentient beings to become free from timidity and weakness?"

Although the Buddha has already revealed the single reality realm with ultimate clarity, he fears that dull-witted sentient beings may still be unable to believe and understand the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Consequently, they would be unable to cultivate the two kinds of contemplative paths;
for this reason, he specifically inquires about them. Furthermore, it is because the Buddha had previously praised his skillful and comforting exposition. △

The second part, the answer, is divided into two sections: first, showing the various skillful modes of exposition; second, clarifying the absence of contradictions. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, a general indication;
second, a specific explanation. Regarding the first:
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha said, "Good son, you should know that for those who have newly begun their studies and resolved their minds to seek the Great [Vehicle]..."
As for those who have not yet attained faith and thus give rise to doubt and timidity regarding the profound Dharma of the unsurpassed path,
I have always used skillful means to proclaim the true meaning and comfort them, causing them to abandon their weakness. For this reason,
I am called the One Who Speaks with Skillful Consolation.

△ Second, the specific explanation of the three [types of consolation]: first, consoling those of small capacity who are timid and weak; second, consoling those who do not understand the intended meaning;

third, consoling those who falsely calculate that things are spontaneous. Those of small capacity who are timid and weak give rise to fear upon hearing that the Mahāyāna is "immediately conventional" (*prajñapti-satya*);

therefore, one consoles them by means of the Mahāyāna being "immediately empty" (*śūnyatā*). Those who do not understand the intended meaning give rise to fear upon hearing that the Mahāyāna is "immediately empty"; therefore, one consoles them by means of... [the Mahāyāna being immediately conventional].

The Mahāyāna is precisely the Middle Way; it consoles those who falsely imagine [the self] to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*), because the meaning of the inherent qualities of the Middle Way arises from such attachment.
Therefore, one consoles them through the cultivation and attainment of the Mahāyāna. Regarding the first of these three sections: first, clarifying timidity; second, clarifying skillful teaching;
third, clarifying the benefits obtained. Now, the first.

What is meant by "consolation"? It refers to sentient beings of dull faculties and small minds who, upon hearing that the Unsurpassed Way is most supreme and most wondrous, feel a longing desire for it in their hearts and resolve to aspire toward it;

yet they further reflect that those who seek the Unsurpassed Way must necessarily accumulate merit to the utmost extent, perform difficult practices and austerities, deliver themselves and others, and endure through vast numbers of kalpas within the cycle of birth and death for a long time.
Only after undergoing diligent toil can one finally attain it. For this reason, a sense of timidity and weakness arises in the mind.
This method of practice in accordance with the nature is taught for those whose inherent disposition leads them to neglect cultivation; it is the gate of perfect existence.
However, those of dull faculties, upon hearing this, will instead form the understanding that it refers to the practice of austerities for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
furthermore, they will give rise to timidity and weakness due to their narrow-mindedness. △ Second, explaining the excellence of the teaching.
I then explained for them the meaning of ultimate reality: that all dharmas are by their very nature empty;
they are ultimately without self, without agent, and without recipient; without self and without other; without action and without arrival; without location or direction;
and without past, present, or future. I further explained the eighteen kinds of emptiness and so forth, wherein there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
Regarding all phenomena that might be perceived as having a fixed, real characteristic, he further explains that all phenomena are like illusions,
like transformations, like the moon reflected in water, like images in a mirror, like a city of the Gandharvas,
like echoes in an empty valley, like sunlight, like bubbles, like dew, like a lamp, like the optical defect of *timira*, like a dream, like lightning, and like clouds. They are merely vexations...
The afflictions and birth-and-death are by nature extremely subtle and weak, and can easily be brought to cessation. Furthermore, afflictions and birth-and-death ultimately have no substance;
they cannot be found when sought. They are originally unarisen and, in reality, there is nothing further to be extinguished. Their self-nature is quiescent, which is itself nirvāṇa.

This is a well-spoken exposition of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) intended to shatter the attachment to existence; it is entirely based on the gate of emptiness within the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), while furthermore relying upon the exposition of the three truths (*tri-satya*).
The initial passage, beginning with "That which is called all dharmas" and continuing through "can be apprehended," [establishes this].

"This refers to the Perfect Ultimate Truth (*pariniṣpanna-paramārtha-satya*). Next, it says 'furthermore, for them he preaches... until they can easily bring [defilements] to cessation,' which refers to the Perfect Conventional Truth (*pariniṣpanna-saṃvṛti-satya*).
Finally, it says 'furthermore, afflictions and birth-and-death... until this is itself nirvāṇa,' which is the Perfect Middle Truth (*pariniṣpanna-madhyama-satya*)."
The initial phrase "all dharmas" refers to the phenomena of the ten realms, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses, and the provisional and real lands.
"Their original nature is inherently empty" means that those produced by conditions lack intrinsic nature.

"Ultimately without self" means that when one investigates the ten realms and all internal and external phenomena, a governing subject cannot be found in reality. "Without action and without reception" means [that there is no agent and no experiencer].
Therefore, I am not a person who receives results through the cause of volitional action (*saṃskāra*). Regarding "neither self nor other":
since there is neither self nor person, one cannot differentiate between self and other. Regarding "no practice and no arrival, no location or direction":
since there is neither actual delusion nor actual awakening, there are no locations such as this shore or the other shore that can be differentiated. Furthermore...
Regarding the absence of past, present, and future: the past has already ceased; the present does not abide; and the future has not yet come into being.

All three periods of time are entirely empty in nature and quiescent. As for the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*): since even "emptiness" is not a single thing, how could there be eighteen?
They are called the eighteen kinds of emptiness because the principle of emptiness is revealed by way of eighteen objects. These are: first, internal [emptiness]...

1. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). 2. External emptiness. 3. Internal-and-external emptiness. 4. Emptiness of emptiness. 5. Great emptiness. 6. Emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). 7. Emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). 8.

Emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). 9. Ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). 10. Emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). 11. Emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*). 12.
Emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). 13. Emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). 14. Emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). 15. Unapprehendable...
One attains emptiness: sixteen, the emptiness of non-existent dharmas; seventeen, the emptiness of existent dharmas;
eighteen, the emptiness of both non-existent and existent dharmas. All dharmas—whether arising and ceasing or nirvana—lack any fixed or real characteristic.

That is to say, within the true and eternal nature, one seeks in vain for coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death, and finds nothing at all to be obtained. This is the first emptiness.
All things are empty; the provisional and the middle are all empty. This is spoken according to the perfectly interfused ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the descriptions of being "like an illusion" or "like a transformation," these are non-existent yet appear to exist; their existence is not substantial existence. The afflictions of the five abodes and the two kinds of birth-and-death are by nature weak and easily extinguished.
This constitutes the "one provisional and all provisional," wherein both the empty and the provisional are all provisional. This is spoken according to the perfectly interfused [truth].
This is an exposition according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Within it, fourteen metaphors are presented;

these are all derived from the six, nine, and ten metaphors, differing only in their appearance and disappearance, or expansion and contraction, yet the meaning remains without increase or decrease. Furthermore, although they collectively encompass the significance of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*), [the underlying intent is one].
All of these serve as antidotes to the grasping at phenomena as truly existent; they nonetheless belong to the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

As for "sunlight," this refers to a mirage (*marīci*), also called a "wild horse" (*gandharva-nagara*). The metaphor of the lamp flame illustrates its ease of extinction; the eye's cataract-like delusion perceives empty flowers;

lightning does not endure long, and clouds appear and vanish with ease. The rest may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, there are the afflictions of the five stages (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*) and the two types of birth-and-death (*dvividha-jāti-maraṇa*).
It takes the single, ultimate reality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) as its essence; therefore, ultimately, no separate self-essence can be found.

This is precisely the quiescent *nirvāṇa* that is neither born nor extinguished. This refers to the "Middle" within all things—wherein emptiness and the conventional are both the Middle—and is explained according to the perfectly integrated Truth of the Middle.
Furthermore, it serves as an antidote to the attachment to phenomena as being substantially real. It returns...
This belongs to the Gate of Emptiness. △ Third, the benefits obtained:
As thus explained, this can destroy all views and diminish the attachments and conceptualizations of one's own body and mind; therefore, one attains freedom from cowardice and weakness.
All things are empty; what is there that is not destroyed? Even nirvāṇa is empty, how much more so the body, mind, emotions, and views!
All are provisional; what is there that is not destroyed? Even nirvāṇa is provisional, how much more so the body, mind, emotions, and views!
All are neither empty nor provisional; what is there that is not destroyed? Birth-and-death and afflictions are all neither empty nor [provisional].

If it is merely provisional, how could there still be a body, mind, emotions, or views? Therefore, it is able to shatter all views and diminish attachments, causing one to abandon the timidity that keeps one far removed from the Buddha-way.
This concludes the first section: Consoling those of small minds who are timid. II. Consoling those who do not understand the intended meaning.
A. First, clarifying the lack of understanding. B. Second, clarifying the skillful teaching. C. Third, clarifying the benefits obtained. (First)

Furthermore, there are three parts: first, directly indicating that [the teaching] is not understood; second, revealing the Buddha’s underlying intent; and third, correctly clarifying erroneous interpretations. Regarding the first:
furthermore, there are sentient beings who, because they do not understand the underlying intent of the Tathāgata’s speech, give rise to timidity and weakness.
△ Second, showing the Buddha’s intended meaning:

One should know that the intended meaning of the Tathāgata’s speech is as follows: because the Tathāgata has already been able to perceive that single reality realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*), he has ultimately attained liberation from all evil dharmas such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, and has realized that *dharmakāya* which is eternal and constant.

This is a collection of immeasurable merits, such as purity, coolness, and immutability. Furthermore, one can clearly perceive that within the bodies of all sentient beings there exist such true, subtle, and pure merits, yet they are shrouded and obstructed by the defilement of the darkness of ignorance.
Consequently, throughout the long night, they constantly undergo the immeasurable sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Regarding this, the Tathāgata...
With a mind of great compassion, he desires to cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and to equally attain the ultimate bliss of the Dharmakāya.
Yet that Dharmakāya is a dharma that is non-discriminative and free from thought;

it can only be attained by those who are able to extinguish false consciousness and perceptions and do not give rise to thoughts. However, all sentient beings constantly delight in discrimination and grasping.
They are attached to all phenomena; because of their inverted and deluded imaginings, they undergo birth and death.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause them to abandon the conceptualization of discriminative attachment, teaches that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence and non-existent, and even all supramundane phenomena are likewise ultimately empty in essence and non-existent. If [this were] expanded...
As for "the teaching," it is like the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), which thus reveal that all phenomena do not depart from the essence of bodhi.
This essence of bodhi is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither non-existent, nor non-non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is not one.
It is not different; it is not non-identical; it is not non-different; it is not both identical and different.
Indeed, ultimately there is not a single characteristic that can be apprehended, because it is free from all characteristics.

To be free from all characteristics means that one cannot grasp it by relying on verbal expression, for within the dharma of bodhi, there is neither one who receives verbal expression nor one who is able to express it.
Therefore, it cannot be known by relying on mental recollection. Within the dharma of Bodhi, there is neither a grasper nor a grasped;

there is no self and no other, for it is free from the marks of conceptual discrimination. If one possesses conceptual thoughts, that is merely false and deceptive, and cannot be called "correspondence" (yoga).
To perceive that single reality-realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*) is to realize the essence of the Middle Way’s true mark (*madhyamā-pratipad-lakṣaṇa*).

To ultimately attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death is to realize the meaning of emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatārtha*). To realize those immeasurable merits is to realize the meaning of non-emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-aśūnyatārtha*).
One personally realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*) and understands that all sentient beings equally possess this.
Because [the Buddha] possesses the secret treasury of the three virtues, he gives rise to great kindness and great compassion, desiring to uproot their suffering and bestow happiness upon them.
For this purpose, he teaches the ultimate, primary emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) so that they may be freed from conceptual discrimination and attachment.
Now, when it is said that all worldly phenomena and all supramundane phenomena are ultimately empty in essence and non-existent, this is precisely...

Because all phenomena—the ten realms, whether provisional or substantial, and whether defiled or pure lands—do not depart from the essence of bodhi, they have no separate intrinsic nature of their own.
This precisely reveals that all things produced by causes and conditions are without exception identical with the Middle Way.
Furthermore, this essence of bodhi is the single, true realm, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the self-nature purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), and the Tathāgata-garbha. This essence...
It is because it is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, and even transcends the characteristics of conceptual discrimination.

To say that the essence of bodhi is not existent means it does not accord with the conceptualizations of the deluded who reckon that birth and death exist. To say that the essence of bodhi is not non-existent means it does not accord with the conceptualizations of the deluded who reckon that there is annihilation and non-being.
To say it is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent means it does not fall into the dualistic proliferation of "neither-nor."
It is not both existent and non-existent, because it does not fall into the category of dualistic contradiction.

It is not identical, because it remains immutable while following conditions to manifest in various ways. It is not different, because it follows conditions without changing, being of a non-dual nature.

It is neither non-identical nor non-different, because it transcends the categories of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is not both identical and different, because it is free from contradiction.
Because of the [four] propositions (*koṭi*). Up to and including the point that ultimately not a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended;
for it does not fall into the characteristics of the four propositions—existence and non-existence, unity and difference, and so forth.

To say that the essence of bodhi is free from all characteristics means that it cannot be grasped by relying on verbal expression, nor can it be known by relying on mental recollection; it is precisely the cessation of the path of language and the mind.

When the sphere of activity ceases, only then is the essential nature of Bodhi revealed. These teachings are fundamentally based on the "neither existent nor empty" gate of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Within this, all three truths are neither existent nor empty; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* extensively clarifies this meaning.
Those who are ignorant do not understand it, and thus they judge it to be a school of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). △ Third, the correct clarification of erroneous interpretations.

Regarding such explanations as these, those sentient beings of dull faculties who are unable to understand them think that the unsurpassed path, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, is merely a dharma of emptiness—absolutely and ultimately non-existent. Their minds become timid and weak;

fearing they will fall into a state of non-attainment, they may give rise to the notion of annihilation, form views of increase or decrease, further develop slander, and disparage themselves while holding others in contempt.

The purpose of negating conceptual attachments is fundamentally to reveal that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-conceptual in essence. However, those of dull faculties misunderstand the words and erroneously interpret them as mere emptiness.

Consequently, they either give rise to fear or conceive of it as annihilation. Those who fear it develop the view of exaggeration (*samāropa*), leading them to engage in slander by claiming it was not spoken by the Buddha.
Those who conceive of it as annihilation develop the view of deprecation (*apavāda*), whereby they disparage themselves and hold others in low esteem.
This refers to returning to annihilation. The first section, clarifying the lack of understanding, is concluded. △ Second, clarifying the correct teaching:
I then explain for them that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is by nature not empty, possesses a true essence, and is replete with immeasurable pure merits and deeds.
From beginningless time, it has been spontaneously perfect; it is neither cultivated nor contrived, even down to a single [moment].
Within the bodies of all sentient beings, it is likewise fully present—unchanging and undifferentiated, without increase or decrease.
This is according to the "Gate of Existence" (you-men) within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which directly reveals the essence of the Middle Way of the Dharmakāya.
Buddhas and sentient beings equally possess it; it is not something that can be annihilated. △ Third, explaining the benefits received.
Such teachings as these are able to eliminate timidity and weakness; this is called "consolation.

Second, the explanation of the meaning of "consolation" regarding the unintelligible is concluded. △ Third, consolation regarding the false calculation of spontaneity has three parts: first, clarifying the false calculation; second, clarifying the skillful teaching;
third, clarifying the attainment of benefit. Now, the first part.
Furthermore, sentient beings who are ignorant and stubbornly attached will also give rise to timidity upon hearing such teachings as these.
Because they grasp at the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as being primordially complete, characterized by neither cultivation nor effort, they give rise to timidity through the perception of non-attainment;
or, calculating it to be spontaneous, they fall into false and inverted views.
One perfects Bodhi and returns to non-attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained, there is nothing that cannot be attained;
