thus, the Great Function manifests before one, and the two benefits are fulfilled. Yet, if one falsely gives rise to the notion of "non-attainment," one will feel timid and weak because there is nowhere for the mind to settle.
Furthermore, if one falsely calculates that birth and Buddhahood are equal and that no cultivation is required, upon hearing [this teaching],...
If it is taught that the very nature of lust, anger, and ignorance is the Buddha-nature, they will then indulge freely in greed and hatred, devoid of shame or remorse.
If they hear it taught that this illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body, they will treasure their own filth and no longer feel weary of or seek to escape it.
If they hear it taught that both the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands, they will remain settled in this mud and silt, seeking no means of deliverance. This is how it should be.
Now, those who discuss the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] are for the most part all falling into this [error]; they are truly pitiable. II. Clarifying the Correct Teaching:
I shall now explain that by practicing all wholesome dharmas, one increases and fulfills them, giving rise to the form-body of the Tathāgata and attaining the pure retribution of immeasurable merit.
This is based on the meaning of the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao), wherein cultivation arises entirely from the nature (*xing*).

It still belongs to the Gate of Existence (*youmen*), serving as an antidote to the view of non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*) and to the perverse, inverted views of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). △ Third, clarifying the benefits obtained.
Such explanations as these cause one to abandon timidity; this is called "consolation.

The first section, which concludes the demonstration of various skillful teachings, is finished. II. Explaining the Avoidance of Contradictory Faults. This has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation;
third, the conclusion. Now, the first part.
The profound meaning that I have taught accords with reality and is free from all faults, because it is spoken without contradiction.
How is it known that it is free from the characteristic of contradiction?
△ Second, the explanation is divided into three parts: first, an explanation to console those who are timid regarding the meaning of emptiness as taught;

second, an explanation to console those who do not understand regarding the meaning of non-emptiness as taught; third, an explanation to console those with false conceptualizations regarding the meaning of cultivation and attainment as taught.
Now, the first part.
That which is called the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, although it is devoid of the sphere of verbal expression, transcends thought and mental recollection, is neither empty nor non-empty,
and is ultimately without any characteristics, cannot be demonstrated by relying on words; yet, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
amidst the illusory causes and conditions of provisional designations, through mutual dependence and correlation, it can be skillfully manifested and explained.
Because that dharmakāya is in its true nature devoid of discrimination, free from self-characteristics and free from other-characteristics, neither empty nor non-empty,
and because it is utterly remote from all characteristics, that dharma-body is said to be ultimately empty and non-existent.
When one is free from the conceptualization of the mind, mental constructions are exhausted; not even a single characteristic can be seen or known by itself as existing.
Therefore, the meaning of emptiness is definitively true, consistent, and unerring.
This clarifies the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as it truly is—emptiness—which corresponds without error to the essence of that garbha.
△ Second, the explanation and consolation regarding the meaning of non-emptiness for those who do not understand.

Furthermore, within that very meaning of emptiness, because one is free from the mental conceptions of discriminative delusion, there is ultimately not a single characteristic that can be said to be empty. Since only the ultimate reality exists, it is therefore non-empty.

That is to say, because one is free from the ideation of consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is no characteristic of falsehood whatsoever; it is ultimately eternal, constant, unchanging, and undifferentiated.
Because there is not a single characteristic that can be destroyed or extinguished, as it is free from increase or decrease.

Furthermore, in that state of non-conceptual reality, which has existed since beginningless time, immeasurable merits and natural activities are spontaneously accomplished and in perfect correspondence.
Because it is neither separated from nor detached [from its qualities], it is said to be "not empty.
This clarifies the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as being truly not empty;

it is precisely manifested from the meaning of true emptiness, and is eternally in correspondence with the essence of the non-conceptual treasury (garbha). △ Third, explaining the consolation for those who harbor false conceptualizations.
Regarding the meaning of cultivation and attainment:
although all sentient beings possess this collection of real entities and virtues, because they are shrouded and obstructed by the cataracts of ignorance, they do not know or see them;
thus, they are unable to realize their virtuous benefits and remain no different from those who have nothing at all.
It is called "non-existent" because, not knowing or seeing the essence of that Dharma, its merits, benefits, and activities cannot be utilized by those sentient beings;

they do not clearly understand their own connection to it. Only by universally practicing all wholesome dharmas, counteracting all obstacles, and seeing that Dharmakāya can one subsequently obtain its merits and benefits. Therefore, it is said that one should practice [the single dharma].
All wholesome dharmas give rise to the Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpakāya*).
This clarifies that the inherent virtues possessed within the Tathāgatagarbha must necessarily rely upon cultivation to be manifested; therefore, they are termed "attained through cultivation.
Furthermore, this does not contradict the essence of equality. To further clarify this by means of an analogy: it is like a room where, from the beginning, there was nothing...
Regarding ghosts, demons, snakes, and insects: though precious gold and silver exist, the blind man does not see them; yet by touching those treasures, he suffers injury.

He falsely imagines there are snakes and demons, becoming distressed and disoriented with fear. Now, to point out that these snakes and demons are fundamentally non-existent is called the meaning of "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*).
That the treasures are fundamentally existent is called the meaning of "reality is not empty" (*tattva-aśūnya*). One must have that blind man depart.
Only when the film of ignorance is removed and the eye of wisdom opened can one then enjoy gold, silver, and precious jewels; this is called the meaning of "cultivated attainment.
Those of the Two Vehicles, by trusting the words of the Tathāgata, know that there are no snakes or ghosts and thus do not give rise to fear; they realize the emptiness [of phenomena].
This is like that blind man sitting dully in the midst of the treasure, failing to touch it; therefore, he cannot perceive the meaning of non-emptiness.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s form-body is like the clarified butter within milk, or the nature of a fifty-foot tree within a *nyagrodha* seed;
it cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. It must depend upon causes and conditions before it is realized.
This concludes the two explanations. △ Third, the conclusion.
"Good son, you should understand that the profound meaning I have explained is definitive, true, and free from the fault of contradiction.
This concludes the second exposition within the section on the correct teaching. Third, the attainment of benefit."

At that time, while the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha was expounding these various supreme, skillful, and profound essential Dharma-gates, one hundred trillion sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and dwelt in the stage of firm faith.
Furthermore, ninety-eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). All the great assembly...
Each offered exquisite celestial incense and flowers to the Buddha and to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.

Having first opened the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*), they were able to know the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*) of the Tathāgata; this is called "arousing the unsurpassed mind" (*anuttara-cittotpāda*).

Their faith and understanding being unshakable, it is called "firm faith" (*dṛḍha-śraddhā*); they are Buddhas of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). Realizing the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching], it is called "attaining the non-arising" (*anutpāda*).

The patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) is the partial realization of Buddhahood. Celestial, wondrous incense and flowers serve as offerings, symbolizing the non-active conditions and causes of the perfect path.
This concludes the section on the formal exposition.
△ Section Three: Dissemination (Three parts). First, the entrustment for upholding; second, the conclusion of the name and meaning of the Dharma; third, the joy of the assembly at that time.
Within the first [part], there are two: first, the entrustment; second, the upholding. Now, the first [of these].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying: "Each of you should receive and uphold this Dharma-gate.
Wherever you reside, cause it to be widely disseminated. Why is this? Such a Dharma-gate is extremely difficult to encounter and is capable of bringing great benefit.
If a person hears the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha and places faith in it..."
Regarding what has been taught: it should be known that such a person will swiftly be able to leave behind all obstacles and quickly reach the unsurpassed path.
"You each, individually, should respectfully exhort others to receive, uphold, and widely disseminate this. Why is this? [The following] explains and establishes the entrustment.

This is an exhortation to the mind. "Swiftly attaining the unsurpassed Way" reveals that this is a perfectly sudden, pure, and wondrous Dharma-gate, unlike the provisional teachings of expedient means. II. Receiving and Upholding.
Thereupon, the great assembly spoke with one voice: "We shall receive and uphold this, disseminate it throughout the world, and dare not allow it to be forgotten.
△ Second, the conclusion of the name and meaning of the Dharma, in two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Now, the first.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Firm Pure Faith addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what is the name of this Dharma-gate within the Sūtra of the Collection of the Six Sense Organs thus spoken? This is the true essence of the Dharma;
I shall receive and uphold it so that all may hear it throughout the final age.”
This was originally requested by the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith on behalf of sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age.
Therefore, he further requested that [the names] be established so that they might be received, upheld, and circulated forever. Because the names are established, the essential truth is revealed;

this "truth" is the substance (*tattva*) of the sutra, and this "essence" is the core principle (*mūla*) of the sutra. Once the core principle and the substance are clarified, the power and function [of the teaching] can then manifest. △ Second, the answer.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith: "This Dharma-gate is named 'Divining and Examining the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma.

It is also named 'Eliminating All Obstacles and Increasing Pure Faith. It is also named 'Revealing the Expedient Means for Those Seeking to Enter the Mahāyāna to Advance Forward,' which manifests the profound, ultimate, and true meaning.
It is also named 'Skillful Consolation,' which causes one to be free from timidity and swiftly [attain liberation]."
Enter the Dharma-gate of the Determination of Firm Faith. You should receive and uphold it according to these names and meanings.

These various names each possess both general and specific meanings. Generally, they constitute a complete exposition of one section, all of which carry the meaning of divining and examining the retributions of good and evil karma, as briefly clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Furthermore, they are all capable of removing obstacles and increasing [virtue].

These are all teachings that reveal the skillful means for advancing toward the Mahāyāna; they are all capable of manifesting the profound, ultimate meaning, and they are all excellent, consoling expositions.
Specifically, the first [section] indicates the method of *Zhancha* (Divination/Investigation), which is called "Investigating the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma.
It indicates the method of practicing repentance within the second wheel, which is called "Eliminating All Obstacles and Increasing [Virtue]."

"Pure faith" refers to the second [point], which indicates the meaning of advancing toward [the goal]; it is termed "revealing and teaching" because it seeks and directs one toward the Mahāyāna, manifesting the profound, ultimate, and true meaning.
It refers to the third [point], which indicates skillful exposition; it is termed "skillfully comforting exposition" because it causes one to abandon timidity and weakness.
Taken together, these general and specific meanings all cause one to swiftly enter the dharma-gate of firm faith and certainty.

Furthermore, the two characters "Zhan" (divination) and "Cha" (examination) establish the name according to its school (*zong*). "The retribution of good and evil karma" establishes the name according to its essence (*ti*).

"Eliminating all obstacles and increasing pure faith" establishes the name according to its function (*yong*). "Revealing the expedient means for those seeking to advance toward the Mahāyāna" establishes the name according to its school.
"Manifesting the profound, ultimate, and true meaning" establishes the name according to its essence. Good...
It provides consolation and speech that causes one to abandon timidity and weakness. It establishes a name based on its function:

it is a gateway to the dharma of swift entry into firm faith and certainty, which is also named according to its function while simultaneously revealing the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna teachings. Second, the conclusion of the explanation of the name and meaning of the dharma.
△ At these three times the assembly rejoiced.
When the Buddha had finished proclaiming the name of this Dharma-door, the entire great assembly was filled with joy; they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
It is for three reasons that there is joy, as can be understood from the usual [explanations].

I recall the winter of the Xinwei year, when I was staying at Northern Tianmu. There, the lay practitioner Xu Yuhai of Wenling—whose Dharma name is Hongkai—spoke to me of this wondrous scripture, the *Zancha*.
I then commissioned someone to go specifically to Yunqi to request a copy of the book.
Upon opening and reading it for the first time, my feelings were a mixture of sorrow and joy. In the winter of the Guiyou year, I was staying at West Lake in Jinting.

At the temple, I established a ritual of repentance based on the sutras. In the early summer of the year Yi-hai, while staying at Jicheumam Hermitage by Wusu Stream, I gave lectures on the topical divisions [of the text].
At that time, I formed the aspiration to compose a commentary; however, due to the overlapping demands of illness and busy affairs, I was unable to fulfill this wish.

Counting back fifteen years from now, I have already provided commentaries for the Brahmajāla Sūtra, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the Lotus Sūtra. Yet, this long-cherished vow remains alone unfulfilled.
It has not yet been fully repaid; this too is truly lamentable. This year, Gengyin, I have already reached fifty-two years of age in this world.

All worldly desires have been extinguished like ashes. Coincidentally, several like-minded companions have come to the Zang Hall on North Mount Tianmu to observe the summer retreat and investigate the Vinaya with earnest resolve.

I reflect that in these末法 (mofa) times, those who wish to attain the pure precepts must set aside the *Zhancha shan'e yebao jing lun* (The Treatise on the Divination Wheel for Examining Good and Evil Retribution).
The Dharma of characteristics has no other path. Thus, I took up my brush on the first day of the sixth month and completed the draft on the fourteenth.
